profiles.label: BMW M Roadster & M Coupe (Z3 M, E36/7 & E36/8, 1998-2002)
profiles.framing: A characterful fair-weather weekend and daily driver, NOT a collector or investment car. The buyer values reliability, condition, driving engagement, value, and proximity to Carmel / Monterey / Bay Area. All Z3 M cars are factory manual. Identify the engine: 1998-2000 = S52 (more robust); 2001-2002 = S54 (rod-bearing design flaw, VANOS failures common and costly).
profiles.weak_points: REAR SUBFRAME / trunk-floor differential-mount cracking or tearing (worst on the M; inspect from below AND the trunk spot welds; reinforcement plates are the fix). S54: rod bearings (preventive replacement with upgraded bearings + oil analysis), double-VANOS failures. S52: cooling system, VANOS rattle. Finned differential mounts. Valve-cover and oil filter housing leaks. Rear trailing-arm bushings. Window regulators. Convertible-top mechanism (roadster). Cluster pixels. Cracked dashboard. Rust at rockers/floors.
profiles.immediate_repairs: cooling-system refresh, tires, fluids, oil analysis (S54)
profiles.repairs_12mo: rod bearings (S54, if not documented), VANOS service, rear subframe reinforcement, clutch if worn
profiles.market_notes: M coupes are the most valuable Z3 variant by a wide margin, with S54 coupes at the top. Documented rod-bearing and subframe work materially raises value. Mileage matters less than documentation on these cars.
profiles.catchup_notes: Cooling regardless of mileage; S54 rod bearings; VANOS; motor/trans mounts; rear shock mounts; tires by date; soft top; A/C. Salvage cars need pre/post-loss photos, invoices, the branding reason, measurements, airbag confirmation, CA smog feasibility, and a specialist PPI covering collision repair and the rear structure.

profiles.label: BMW 135i Convertible (E88, N54 & N55)
profiles.framing: This is the cheap-thrills, short-wheelbase BMW: 300 hp turbo six in a small rear-drive chassis, and in E88 convertible form a genuinely usable top-down daily for Highway 1 and the Monterey Peninsula. For this buyer it is a driver, not an asset — E88 verts sit at the bottom of the 1-Series price ladder while carrying the same running costs as a much more expensive car. The whole exercise is buying maintenance history, not miles: a documented, unmodified, tune-free car with cooling, fuel and turbo work already paid for is worth several thousand dollars more than a cheap one. Salt-free California/Southwest history and a top that has been exercised and drained matter as much as the drivetrain.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Fuel system, N54 cars (2008–2010): the HPFP (high-pressure fuel pump) was the subject of multiple recalls and an extended 10yr/120k warranty that has now expired on every car; symptoms are long cranks, limp mode, 'Half Engine Power' warning, rough cold running. Replacement is roughly $900–1,400. Piezo injectors on N54 failed in waves (index 11/12 supersessions); a full set is $1,500–2,500 installed. 2) N55 cars (2011–2013) use solenoid injectors and a more robust pump but still fail individually — a misfiring cylinder usually means one injector at $250–450 plus labor. 3) Turbocharger wastegate rattle: N54 twin turbos develop wastegate flutter, N55's single twin-scroll turbo develops the same rattle in its electric wastegate actuator, typically past 60–90k miles; audible as a metallic buzz at light throttle 1,500–2,500 rpm and eventually underboost codes. Actuator alone $600–900, turbo replacement $2,500–4,000. 4) Cooling system is consumable, not durable: the electric water pump and thermostat are a 60–90k mile / 8-year item at $900–1,400 together; the plastic expansion tank, coolant hoses and the plastic thermostat housing crack with age. A car with no cooling records at 50k+ miles and 13 years should be assumed to need the whole job. 5) Oil leaks are near-universal by 60–80k: valve cover and VCG gasket ($600–900), oil filter housing gasket ($500–800, contaminates the belt if ignored), and the oil pan gasket ($1,200–1,800 due to subframe clearance). Look for oil on the exhaust manifold and a smell after a hard drive. 6) Direct injection carbon buildup on intake valves: expect walnut blasting every 60–80k miles, $500–900. Symptoms are rough cold idle, misfires under load, mild power loss. 7) The stock plastic charge pipe (both N54 and N55) cracks at the coupler and dumps boost; an aluminum replacement is a sensible, accepted fix — but confirm it accompanied a stock tune, not a boost increase. 8) Tuning/modification is the biggest hidden risk: heavily tuned N54/N55 cars suffer crank hub timing slip, burned pistons, and stretched rod bearings. Any car with a JB4/MHD/Cobb history, upgraded turbos, or a methanol kit should be treated as a rebuild candidate unless the tune history is fully documented and the crank hub pinned. 9) DCT (7-speed GS7D36SG) cars need a mechatronic/clutch fluid service every ~60k miles ($500–800); neglected units show shudder from a stop and eventually mechatronic sleeve leaks or clutch wear — $3,500–6,000 to fix. Manual cars: check clutch and the dual-mass flywheel ($1,500–2,200) and the notorious weak 6-speed synchro feel when cold. 10) Convertible-specific: hydraulic top cylinders and pump leak (fluid on the trunk liner or top well), microswitches/Hall sensors fail and cause the top to stop mid-cycle, and the roll-over bar deployment mechanism can seize. Top mechanism repairs run $800–3,000; a replacement top with glass window is $1,500–2,500 installed. 11) Blocked convertible/cowl drain tubes are the classic cause of wet front footwells and trunk, which then kills body modules and the FRM (footwell module) — a wet-carpet car is a $1,000+ electrical rabbit hole. 12) Suspension and rubber age out: front control arm bushings and rear trailing arm/rear shock mounts around 70–100k ($800–1,500 for a front refresh), plus run-flat-battered wheels and struts. 13) Electrical odds and ends: FRM module failure (windows/lights all dead, coding recovery ~$300–600), Comfort Access door handle sensors, iDrive/CIC screen and CD stereo faults, and the E88 dash leather delaminating around the airbag seam (cosmetic, $500–1,500 to re-wrap). 14) Brakes on M Sport cars use larger rotors and pads that wear fast if driven hard; budget $900–1,400 for a four-corner refresh.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid service including engine oil, brake fluid and (if DCT) transmission/mechatronic fluid; new coolant if age is unknown. Replace the cracked/aged plastic charge pipe and boost hoses if still stock. Clear and flush all four convertible/cowl drain tubes and dry/verify the trunk and footwells. Address any known oil weep (valve cover or filter housing gasket) before it fouls the belt. Fresh non-run-flat tires and an alignment; new wiper blades and cabin filter; battery test with registration if replaced. Expect $1,500–3,000 on a decent 50–70k mile car.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Electric water pump and thermostat if not documented ($900–1,400); intake valve walnut blasting ($500–900); one or more fuel injectors ($300–600 each installed); turbo wastegate actuator if rattle is developing ($600–900); front control arm bushings and possibly rear shock mounts ($800–1,500); brake pads/rotors ($900–1,400); convertible top hydraulic seal or microswitch repair ($400–1,200); oil filter housing and/or oil pan gasket ($500–1,800).
profiles.market_notes: Manual coupes (E82) command the strongest money and 135is/6MT cars are the top of the market; DCT convertibles are the value end — typically $3,000–6,000 behind an equivalent manual coupe. N55 cars (2011–2013) generally bring more than N54 for perceived fuel-system reliability, though N54 enthusiasts pay up for unmodified, well-documented examples. Miles matter less than binders: a 70k-mile car with pump/injector/turbo/cooling receipts beats a 45k-mile car with 'no records.' Rare colors like Marrakesh Brown over Terracotta, Le Mans Blue, and Alpine White with M Sport/Sport seats add appeal; heavily tuned, deleted, or accident-history cars are discounted hard and are difficult to resell.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 12–16 year old E88 needs a full age-based catch-up regardless of mileage: coolant system components, all gaskets and rubber hoses, suspension bushings, brake fluid and likely a battery, plus convertible top seals, drains and hydraulics. Low-mileage cars are often worse for rubber and top mechanisms because they have sat. Budget $3,000–5,000 in the first year on top of the purchase price to get a typical example to a trustworthy baseline.

profiles.label: BMW 3 Series E30 (325e/325i/325is, M20 six-cylinder)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the E30 325is is a compact, analog, rear-drive coupe meant to be driven on Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road most weekends — light (2,700 lb), hydraulically steered, with a smooth M20B25 six and a shift linkage that rewards patience. It is not a fast car by modern standards; the appeal is transparency, small footprint, and a parts/knowledge ecosystem that makes long-term ownership realistic. Because these are now 35-40 years old, condition, rust history, and a paper trail matter far more than the odometer reading, and a documented, unmodified, uncracked-dash car with the sport seats and LSD is worth a real premium over a 'clean-looking' unknown. Coastal California living means salt air and damp — a car that has never lived in the Rust Belt is materially more valuable to this buyer than one that spent 30 years in Nebraska or the Northeast.
profiles.weak_points: 1) M20 timing belt and water pump: the M20B25 is an interference engine — a snapped belt bends valves and turns a $400 service into a $3,500-$6,000 head rebuild. Interval is 60k miles or 4-5 years, whichever comes first, and the water pump (early cars used a plastic impeller that disintegrates) and tensioner should go with it. Demand a dated receipt or photo of a chalk-marked belt; if there is no proof, assume it must be done immediately regardless of mileage. 2) Cylinder head cracking between the valve seats on early M20 heads (casting numbers 1277731 and 885) — symptoms are unexplained coolant loss, overheating, or a milky film; a later 1705310 or 1710891 head or a documented replacement is a plus. Head work runs $1,800-$3,500. 3) Cooling system generally: the plastic-neck radiator, expansion tank, thermostat housing, and hoses all become brittle at 25+ years. Any overheating episode on an M20 is a head-gasket/head-crack event waiting to happen. Budget $600-$1,200 for a full cooling refresh. 4) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket, and the front timing cover/oil pan seams weep on nearly every car; the rear main and oil pan gasket ($700-$1,200 with subframe drop on the pan) are the expensive ones. Check for oil pooling on the exhaust and on the crossmember. 5) Fuel system: the 30+ year old rubber fuel hoses under the car and at the tank, plus the fuel pump and accumulator, are a genuine fire risk on cars with unknown history. Original-looking cracked hoses = replace now, $300-$800. 6) Rust: shock towers (look under the strut mount hats in the engine bay for bubbling or cracking), the battery tray corner in the trunk, the rear subframe/trailing-arm mounting points and floor, rear wheel arches, jack points, sunroof drains and the panel under the rear window seal, and the seam behind the front fenders. A Midwest/Northeast car needs the underside and trunk floor photographed thoroughly. Structural shock-tower or subframe-mount rot is a walk-away or a $3,000+ repair. 7) Interior plastics: cracked dashboard is near-universal ($400-$900 for a good used one plus labor, more for a re-skin), sagging headliner, brittle door cards, failing window regulator clips, and disintegrating sunroof cassette parts. Sport seat bolsters on 325is cars split at the driver's outer bolster; the beige and Cardinal interiors are hardest to source. 8) Suspension and steering bushings: front control arm bushings and ball joints, rear trailing arm bushings (RTABs, cause of vague rear end and inconsistent toe), subframe bushings, sway bar links, and the steering box/center link/idler arm all wear out by 100k. A full front-and-rear refresh with shocks is $1,500-$3,000 installed. Note whether 'shocks replaced' also included struts, mounts, and bump stops or was just dampers. 9) Electrical: the instrument cluster and OBC use failure-prone capacitors and cracked solder joints — dead odometer gears (a black-and-white speedometer needle drift or stuck odo), dim pixel displays in the OBC/SI board, and the SI battery packs that leak onto the board. Cluster odometer gear repair $150-$400. Also check the sunroof motor, central locking pneumatics (early) or actuators, and the notoriously melting relay panel connections. 10) Getrag 260 transmission and driveline: synchros (especially 2nd) start to balk when cold at high miles, the shift linkage bushings and selector rod joint make the shifter sloppy ($100 in parts, big improvement), the giubo/flex disc cracks, the center support bearing collapses (vibration at 45-60 mph), and the guide tube/throwout bearing squeal precedes a clutch job. Clutch/flywheel/rear main combined job runs $1,400-$2,500. 11) Limited-slip differential: the 25% ZF LSD on a 325is wears out and behaves like an open diff; check for one-wheel spin and for gear whine or leaking diff cover/output seals. Diff rebuild or swap $800-$2,000. 12) Brakes and ABS: the ABS control unit and wheel sensors fail, the master cylinder and rear calipe
profiles.immediate_repairs: Timing belt, tensioner, water pump, thermostat, and all coolant hoses unless there is dated proof within 4 years; full fluid service (engine, Getrag 260 with MTL, diff, brake fluid, coolant); replace all rubber fuel lines and check the fuel pump/accumulator; new tires if date codes exceed ~6 years regardless of tread (the Uniroyal Tigerpaws on the example car are a red flag for age); shift linkage bushings and selector rod; flex disc/giubo and center support bearing if there is any driveline vibration; front control arm bushings and ball joints; battery, belts, and a check/clean of the relay panel and grounds.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Rear trailing arm bushings and subframe bushings; rear shock mounts and bump stops; clutch, throwout bearing, guide tube and rear main seal if any squeal or slip; oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets; radiator if still original plastic-neck; instrument cluster odometer gears and SI board battery service; sunroof cassette lubrication and drain clearing; A/C evaluation and likely condenser/dryer/expansion valve refresh; LSD evaluation and possible clutch pack rebuild; dash cap or replacement dash and headliner if sagging; seat bolster repair.
profiles.market_notes: The 325is coupe with 5-speed and factory LSD sits near the top of the non-M E30 hierarchy, above 325i sedans and well above 325e/eta cars; convertibles and 325ix occupy separate niches. Documented low-mileage, unmodified, rust-free cars with original paint, intact uncracked dash, and books/window sticker/records bring the strongest numbers; a Carfax accident, a replaced fender tag, or a repaint drops a car into the driver-grade band. Delphin Gray, Alpine White, Diamond Schwarz and Zinnoberrot are safe; beige/Pearl Beige leather is desirable when clean but expensive to fix when it is not. Modified cars (M50/S52 swaps, coilovers, aftermarket wheels, non-original seats) can be cheaper to buy and are much harder to resell to the documentation-driven auction crowd; typical strong-driver money for a 90k-110k mile 325is is roughly $12k-$20k, with exceptional preserved examples going higher.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 35-40 year old E30 needs a systems catch-up regardless of mileage: every rubber item — coolant hoses, fuel lines, suspension bushings, engine mounts, tires — ages out on the calendar, not the odometer, and low-mileage cars are often worse for seized calipers and dried seals. Budget $3,000-$5,000 in the first year for timing belt/cooling, fuel lines, bushings, and fluid services even on a well-kept car, plus a contingency for the cluster, sunroof, and A/C.

profiles.label: BMW 3 Series Touring (E91 328i / 328xi Wagon)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the E91 is the classic do-everything answer: a normally aspirated inline-six wagon with a real manual option, hatch practicality for Monterey Peninsula weekends, and enough chassis feel to make Highway 1 and Laureles Grade worth driving. It is a $10k–$25k car with $60k-car maintenance costs, so the value case lives or dies on records: cooling system, VANOS, gaskets, suspension, and (on autos) transmission fluid. Because it is a driver, not an investment, condition and documented catch-up work matter more than mileage. In California the emissions story is decisive — SULEV N51 cars, engine swaps, and deleted/tuned hardware all interact with biennial smog and BAR rules.
profiles.weak_points: Cooling system is the signature E9x expense: the electric water pump and its associated thermostat are effectively a 60–90k-mile wear item, and failure is often abrupt (limp mode, overheat warning). Budget $900–$1,400 installed for pump plus thermostat; ask for a dated invoice, not 'recently done.' The plastic coolant expansion tank, upper/lower hose necks, and radiator end tanks go brittle by 10–12 years and weep or split; a full refresh is $600–$1,200. The N52's magnesium-alloy block is durable but leaks: the valve cover (plastic, warps) and its gasket, the oil filter housing gasket, and the oil pan gasket are near-universal by 90–130k. Valve cover $500–$900; oil filter housing gasket $500–$900 and important because oil drips onto the serpentine belt — a shredded belt can be pulled into the front crank seal and cause catastrophic damage. VANOS solenoids and the VANOS bolts/exhaust adjustment unit cause rough cold idle, a 2A87/2A82 code and lazy throttle; solenoids are cheap, a full VANOS unit is $800–$1,500. The DISA intake flap valve can shed its plastic pivot into the intake — $250–$400 to replace, cheap insurance. Valve stem seals are the classic N51/N52 sin: a puff of blue smoke on cold start or after long idle, especially on California SULEV N51 cars, and a head-off-optional-but-expensive job at $2,000–$3,500. Watch smog readiness monitors and NOx-related codes on N51 cars. Wagon-specific: the tailgate glass hinges crack and the rear hatch wiring loom chafes inside its rubber boot, causing dead wiper, dead lock, dead lights and intermittent tailgate release; hinges $400–$900, loom repair $200–$500. Rear light cluster and hatch seals leak into the spare-wheel well — pull the trunk floor and look for standing water, rust, and a corroded battery cable or amplifier if so equipped. Panoramic roof cassettes are heavy and troublesome: blocked drains dump water into the headliner and A/B-pillar carpets, and the cassette slide/cable can fail ($1,000–$2,500). Suspension bushings are consumables: front control arm/thrust arm bushings, rear trailing arm bushings and rear shock mounts all knock and wander by 80–120k; a full front and rear refresh is $1,200–$2,500. Rear wheel bearings and front hub bearings hum by 100k, $400–$700 each corner. Electrics: the FRM footwell module can brick during a low-voltage jump or battery swap, taking out lights and windows ($300–$800 to repair/recode); the FSU/blower final stage resistor kills fan speeds; and the battery must be registered when replaced or charging strategy cooks the new one. On manuals, the shift shaft seal leaks gear oil onto the underbody, the clutch delay valve is commonly deleted, and clutch plus dual-mass flywheel is $1,800–$3,000. On the 6HP19 automatic, the 'lifetime' fluid is not — unserviced units at 120k+ show flare and harsh 2-3 shifts; fluid and pan/filter service is $500–$800 and the mechatronic sleeve/adapter leak is a common $600–$1,200 job. Finally, run-flat tires and 18-inch wheels crack rims and beat the bushings; check for bent/repaired wheels and consider non-runflats.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Oil service with a real BMW-spec 5W-30, coolant condition test and expansion tank/hose inspection, full fault-code scan with freeze-frame, battery test and registration if replaced, serpentine belt and pulleys if any oil-filter-housing weep is present, DISA valve inspection, sunroof drain flush, tailgate loom and hinge inspection, alignment plus four matched tires if staggered/mismatched, and rear brake pads/rotors (BMW pads wear rears first).
profiles.repairs_12mo: Electric water pump and thermostat if not documented within 60k miles, valve cover gasket and oil filter housing gasket, front control arm bushings and possibly rear shock mounts/trailing arm bushings, VANOS solenoid cleaning or replacement, automatic transmission fluid and pan/filter (or manual shift shaft seal), one or two wheel bearings, expansion tank and radiator hoses, and window regulator or FSU blower resistor as they surface.
profiles.market_notes: Manual-transmission 328i wagons are the enthusiast currency here and carry a meaningful premium over slushbox cars — a clean documented 6-speed can bring double an equivalent automatic. Sport package with the proper seats, xDrive (valued in snow markets, less so in Carmel), Montego Blue/Space Gray/Alpine White over saddle or black, and non-panoramic roofs all help; heavy modification, engine swaps, salvage history, and 150k+ miles compress value fast. Records are worth more than mileage: a 130k car with a folder of cooling, VANOS and suspension invoices should outbid a 90k car with no history. Cars with California-legal emissions status (stock N51/N52 with intact CARB-legal hardware) are worth a clear premium locally because a swapped or tuned car may be unregisterable without a BAR referee sticker.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 110–140k-mile E91 is due for a cooling-system refresh, the standard trio of oil leaks (valve cover, filter housing, pan), and a round of front and rear bushings — plan $3,000–$5,000 of deferred catch-up in the first year unless invoices prove otherwise. Rubber and plastic are the real age items on a 13–18 year old car: hoses, mounts, sunroof drains, hatch loom, and window regulators. Buying the car with the thickest documented folder is cheaper than buying the lowest-mileage example.

profiles.label: BMW Z3 Coupe (E36/8, incl. M Coupe)
profiles.framing: The 'clown shoe' is a short-wheelbase, stiff-shell hatchback built on E36 Z3 running gear — a genuinely rare, characterful weekend and back-road car for Carmel/Highway 1 and Laureles Grade duty, not a commuter. For this buyer it is an enthusiast bridge car: manual, unmodified, documented, and bought on chassis integrity rather than on shine. Values now split sharply between the S52/S54 M Coupe and the 2.8/3.0i coupe, so verifying exactly which car is in front of you is step one. Because the E36/8 has a known structural weak point (rear subframe mounting area), evidence of a clean underbody inspection outranks cosmetics, mileage, or 'like new' claims.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Rear subframe mounting points: the trunk floor sheetmetal where the rear subframe bolts up can crack, tear, or deform — the single most important E36/8 issue, disproportionately on M Coupes and any car driven hard or on sticky tires/lowered stiff suspension. Symptoms are hairline cracks radiating from the four mount cups, paint flaking, sealant splitting, or a 'clunk/wander' under load. Reinforcement plates (Redish, Vincebar, or BMW dealer plates) welded in run $2,000–$4,000; repairing already-torn metal $4,000–$7,000+. Look for photos of the trunk floor with carpet and spare tire out, and receipts naming the shop and plate kit. 2) Cooling system (M52TU 2.8 and M54 3.0i): plastic-necked radiator, expansion tank, thermostat housing, and water pump with plastic impeller are all life-limited at 60–100k miles or ~10–12 years, whichever comes first — regardless of odometer, a 25-year-old car on original cooling parts is a roadside failure waiting to happen. Full refresh $900–$1,800. A cooked M52TU/M54 head from an overheat is a $4,000+ event. 3) VANOS: rattle at idle/light throttle, lazy low-end torque; seal kit (Beisan) $200 DIY, $700–$1,200 at a shop. S54 M Coupes have the more complex, more expensive double-VANOS. 4) S54 rod bearings (2001–2002 M Coupe only): the well-known interval item; without a documented bearing service (~$2,000–$3,500 with rod bolts and oil analysis), assume it's due. Also check for the BMW VANOS/rod-bearing recall history and oil-pump nut/shaft. 5) Oil leaks: valve cover gasket, oil filter housing gasket, and oil pan gasket all weep by 80–120k miles; $400–$1,200 each depending on access. Look for oil on the exhaust manifold and burning smell. 6) Crankcase ventilation (CCV/oil separator) on M54 3.0i and M52TU: clogged separator causes smoke, rough idle, and can pull the dipstick out; $400–$800. 7) Driveline mounts and bushings: rear differential bushings and diff mount, driveshaft flex disc (guibo) and center support bearing, and rear trailing arm bushings all age out and cause clunks and driveline shudder; $800–$2,000 to do the set. Original diff-mount failures also contribute to subframe stress. 8) Rear hatch and glass sealing: the coupe leaks into the spare-tire well through the hatch seal, third brake light, and taillight gaskets — pull the trunk carpet and look for staining, rust, or a musty smell; the water also feeds subframe corrosion. Hatch struts sag ($100). 9) Interior electrics/trim: instrument cluster pixel loss (cluster rebuild $150–$350), sticky soft-touch coating on console/vents, sagging headliner, window regulator clips, and glovebox/ashtray plastics. Parts for coupe-specific trim (rear side glass, hatch, cargo cover, rear panels) are scarce and expensive. 10) ABS/ASC module and wheel-speed sensors: dashboard triangle plus ABS light; module rebuild $250–$500, sensors $100 each. 11) Secondary air pump and DISA valve (M54): CEL codes P0491/P0492 and a rattling DISA flap; $250–$600. 12) Clutch and hydraulics: clutch typically 100–140k miles; slave/master cylinders leak with age. Clutch job $1,400–$2,200 due to transmission removal. 13) Suspension bushings and shocks: front control arm bushings, rear shock mounts (RSMs) and their reinforcement, and 25-year-old dampers — a full refresh with quality parts is $1,500–$2,500. Many coupes have been lowered on coilovers with big wheels, which accelerates subframe and RSM damage. 14) Rust: California cars are usually clean, but East Coast/Midwest examples rot at the rear fender arches, rockers, jack points, trunk floor seams, and the subframe area itself — this is a specific problem for the listed New York car. Bushing replacement is not evidence of structural soundness; the trunk-floor welds and differential mounting area are a separate inspection and a separate repair (https://www.autoengineering.com/portfolio/bmw-z3-rear-subframe-mounting-points-repair/).
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full underbody/trunk-floor inspection with the carpet and spare out, and reinforcement plates if any cracking is found ($2,000–$4,000). Complete cooling-system refresh if not documented within 8 years/60k miles (radiator, expansion tank, thermostat, hoses, water pump) $900–$1,800. All fluids including differential and manual gearbox, plus brake fluid flush ($400–$700). New tires if the 19s are period no-name rubber, and ideally a return to a correct-offset 17-inch M Coupe/OEM-style wheel and OE-spec suspension ($1,500–$3,000). Reseal the hatch/taillight gaskets and clear the trunk drains ($200–$500). Battery, wipers, and a full pre-drive brake inspection.
profiles.repairs_12mo: VANOS seal kit and DISA/CCV service ($700–$1,500). Valve cover and oil filter housing gaskets ($700–$1,400). Guibo, center support bearing, diff and trailing arm bushings ($1,000–$2,000). Shocks and rear shock mounts if not recently done ($1,200–$2,000). Cluster pixel repair and window regulator clips ($300–$600). On a 2001–02 S54 car, budget rod bearings and a valve adjustment ($2,500–$4,000). Clutch and hydraulics if the pedal is high or shudders ($1,600–$2,200).
profiles.market_notes: The market is bimodal: S52/S54 M Coupes are collector cars ($45k–$100k+ depending on year, color, and records), while 2.8/3.0i coupes are enthusiast cars typically $18k–$32k, with the 2001–02 3.0i manual at the top. Documented subframe reinforcement, a rust-free Western car, factory wheels, and a thick service file add real money; lowered coilovers, 19-inch wheels, aftermarket exhaust, and repainted or Bondo'd rear arches subtract it. Rare factory colors (Imola Red, Estoril Blue, Titanium Silver, Hell Red) and clean two-tone leather help; black-on-black with modifications is the commodity spec. Automatic 2.8 coupes trade at a meaningful discount and are hard to resell; low mileage without records is worth far less than average mileage with them.
profiles.catchup_notes: Assume a 25-year-old, low-mileage example needs age-based rather than mileage-based work: every cooling component, all rubber (hoses, bushings, guibo, motor and trans mounts), fuel lines, brake fluid and possibly calipers, tires regardless of tread, and seals that have dried out from sitting. Budget $3,000–$5,000 in the first year on a nice non-M coupe just to make it a trustworthy Highway 1 driver, plus the subframe reinforcement if not already done.

profiles.label: BMW Z3 Roadster & Coupe (E36/7, E36/8)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the Z3 is a cheap-to-buy, analog, rear-drive weekend roadster for Highway 1 and Carmel Valley Road — hydraulic steering, a real handbrake, an inline-six, and a top that drops in fifteen seconds. A 2002 is the last and best year: M54 2.5i/3.0i engines, updated interior, and the wide rear track. It is emphatically not an investment car (M Roadster/M Coupe excepted), so buy the best-documented, unmolested six-cylinder manual you can find and treat the purchase price as the smaller half of the equation. Coastal fog, salt air, and a 20+ year old convertible top mean condition and storage history matter more here than mileage.
profiles.weak_points: Rear subframe mounting points: the single most important Z3 issue. The floor pan sheet metal around the four differential/subframe mounts tears and cracks, especially on 2.8/3.0i/M cars and any car that saw autocross, hard launches, or a heavy tow hitch. It is often invisible until you pull the trunk carpet and spare and inspect the sheet metal from above, or get under the car and look at the seams around the mounts. Repair is a welded reinforcement kit (Turner/Redish Motorsport/AKG plates) at roughly $2,000–$4,500 depending on how far the tears have propagated; ignoring it eventually means a floor pan section. Ask for photos of bare metal at all four mounts. Cooling system: M52TU/M54 cooling parts are plastic and time-expired at 20 years — radiator end tanks, expansion tank, thermostat housing, water pump (plastic impeller on some), and the radiator neck all fail without warning and an overheat can warp the aluminum head ($3,000+). A full cooling refresh is $700–$1,200 in parts and should be treated as a maintenance interval, not a repair; look for receipts within the last 8 years/60k miles. VANOS: M52TU/M54 single/double VANOS uses O-rings and seals that harden, producing a diesel-like rattle at idle, weak low-end torque, and rough cold running; seal kits are $150 in parts, $600–$900 installed, and a rebuilt unit is $1,000+. Crankcase ventilation (CCV/oil separator): the M54's CCV diaphragm and heater hoses crack, causing high crankcase vacuum, whistling, oil consumption, sucked-out rear main seal, and rough idle; $400–$700 to do properly with all the hoses. Oil filter housing gasket and valve cover gasket: near-universal leaks by 100k, oil drips onto the exhaust manifold and makes the classic BMW hot-oil smell; $300–$600 each. DISA valve (M54): the intake manifold flap pivot fails and can shed plastic into the engine; rebuild kit or replacement, $150–$350. Convertible top: the rear plastic window yellows, cracks and separates from the fabric; the top itself shrinks and the frame pivots seize. A quality Haartz cloth top with glass window installed is $1,200–$2,000, and a torn rear window on a coastal car means a wet interior and a rusting floor. Check the drain channels behind the seats. Rust and water intrusion: inspect rocker panels below the doors, the rear wheel arch lips, the seams under the sill trim, the trunk floor/spare well, and the battery tray (battery lives in the trunk on the passenger side); trunk lid seal and taillight gaskets leak and quietly rot the trunk pan. Electrical/interior: instrument cluster and OBC LCD pixel loss (a $150–$250 refurb), failing door lock actuators/microswitches, window regulators, and the notorious brittle interior trim; the headliner in the Coupe sags. Seats: driver's seat bolster and base foam collapse, and the seat frame bushings squeak; a re-foam and reupholster is $600–$1,200. Suspension/steering: front control arm (thrust arm) bushings and tie rods are 60–80k-mile items that cause shimmy under braking; rear shock mounts crack; original dampers on any surviving example are long dead. Budget $1,200–$2,000 for a full front-end and damper refresh. Driveline: hydraulic clutch master/slave cylinders weep and leave a soft pedal ($300–$500); the rear differential bushing and the driveshaft center support bearing/flex disc (guibo) fail with vibration at 60–80 mph ($500–$900). Fuel: level sender and in-tank pump failures give erratic gauge readings and hot-start issues. Secondary air pump and its check valve fail and throw P0491/P0492 codes that will block a smog pass — plan $400–$700. Finally, the 1.9L four (M44) is slow, weaker in resale, and shares the timing chain guide and cooling issues without the six's charm; a four-cylinder 2002 does not exist in the US, so a 2002 will be a 2.5i, 3.0i, or M.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full cooling system refresh (radiator, expansion tank, thermostat, water pump, hoses, cap) unless documented recent; oil service with a proper BMW filter; CCV/oil separator and hose set on the M54; oil filter housing and valve cover gaskets if seeping; convertible top rear window or full top if cracked/hazed plus clearing the top-well drains; four matching date-coded tires (age-outs are common on low-mile cars); front control arm bushings and tie rods if there is any shimmy; battery and trunk battery-tray cleanup; brake fluid flush.
profiles.repairs_12mo: VANOS seal service if the rattle is present; DISA valve rebuild; shocks/struts and rear shock mounts; clutch hydraulics; driveshaft flex disc, center support bearing and differential bushing; secondary air pump/valve if a smog code appears; instrument cluster pixel repair; door lock actuators and window regulator; seat foam/bolster repair; soft-top frame pivot service and re-lube; exhaust flex section or rear muffler; subframe reinforcement plates preemptively if the car is a 3.0i/M and shows early stress marks.
profiles.market_notes: Six-cylinder manuals carry the market: a documented 2002 3.0i manual with a hardtop, sport package and clean floors is the top of the non-M range, while automatics and the 2.5i sell noticeably softer. M Roadster and especially M Coupe live in a separate, much higher tier and demand S54 rod-bearing and subframe evidence. A factory hardtop adds $1,500–$2,500, and desirable colors (Steel Blue, Topaz Blue, Imola/Hell Red, Titanium Silver) with a contrasting or well-preserved interior move cars fast; grey/black on black with a tired top is the discount end. Records and rust-free southwestern/coastal-garaged provenance are worth more than a low odometer, and mileage below 60k mostly matters for the cosmetics it implies.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 2002 Z3 is a 20+ year old car whose rubber, plastic, and fabric are all time-expired regardless of mileage: expect to spend $3,000–$5,000 in the first year on cooling system, CCV, gaskets, suspension bushings, dampers, tires, and likely the convertible top. None of it is exotic and most is DIY-friendly, but budgeting for it up front is the difference between a delightful cheap roadster and a rolling disappointment.

Rockers under sill trim, rear arch lips, floor pans, trunk pan/spare well, and trunk battery tray for corrosion or damp carpet
Front control arm/thrust arm bushings, tie rods, and steering play; test braking shimmy above 55 mph
Driveshaft flex disc (guibo), center support bearing, and diff bushing — check for 60–80 mph vibration and cracked rubber
Clutch pedal feel and engagement point; inspect master/slave cylinder for weeping and fluid level
Instrument cluster and OBC pixel loss, door lock actuators, window regulators, all warning lamps illuminate then extinguish
OBD-II readiness monitors all set and no pending P0491/P0492 secondary air or catalyst codes
Driver bolster/foam collapse, seat rails and squeaks, dash and door trim cracking, headliner (Coupe)
If a hardtop is included, verify matching color, seals, mounting hardware, and stand
Tire DOT date codes, matched sizes front/rear, rotor lip and pad life, brake fluid condition
Service file continuity, number of owners, garaged/coastal exposure history, matching keys and tool kit presence in trunk

dealbreakers: Salvage, rebuilt, or flood title
Automatic transmission
Unrepaired cracked rear subframe mounts without a price adjustment covering full welded reinforcement
Evidence of overheating or head gasket/head work on the M54 without full documentation
Structural rust in floor pans, rockers, or trunk pan

critical_evidence.label: Clear photos of all four rear subframe/differential mounting points with trunk carpet and spare removed, plus underside seam shots

profiles.label: International Harvester Scout II (incl. Traveler, Terra, SSII)
profiles.framing: This is a hand-built-feeling, body-on-frame 1970s 4x4 that the buyer will drive on the Monterey Peninsula, Carmel Valley Road, and the occasional beach/fire-road run — not a garage queen and not a stock-market substitute. What matters most is metal: a Scout II is essentially a rust-and-documentation purchase wrapped around a very simple, very rebuildable drivetrain. Mechanicals (304/345 V8, TF727 or T-19, Dana 20, Dana 44s) are cheap and well-supported by the aftermarket; a rotten rear quarter, floor, or frame rail is what turns a $29k truck into a $50k truck. Because coastal California air is hard on these, a Scout that has lived near the ocean without proper undercarriage care should be judged more harshly than mileage or cosmetics would suggest.
profiles.weak_points: ["Rear quarter panels and the rear 'kick-up' area behind the rear wheels are the classic Scout II rot zone — the inner/outer quarter sandwich and the rear wheelhouse trap mud and never dry out. Any car described as having 'some typical Scout rust' should be assumed to have this. Proper cut-and-weld repair with quality reproduction panels runs $3,000–$8,000 per side once paint blending is included; bondo-and-fiberglass patches are common and disqualifying at this price point.", 'Floor pans, footwells, and the seat-belt/seat-mount reinforcements rust from the top down (leaking windshield gasket, cowl vent, and door seals) and from the bottom up. Pull the carpet or mats; look for fresh undercoating or seam sealer hiding perforation. Floor pan replacement $1,500–$3,500.', 'Frame: the boxed rails are usually decent but rot at the rear spring hangers, the rear crossmember, and where the body mounts perch. Body mount bushings (12 points) collapse and let the tub shift, causing door-gap and hood-alignment weirdness. New mount kit $150–$400 in parts, a full day of labor; frame rail section repair $2,000–$5,000 and a value cliff.', 'Tailgate, rear hatch/glass frame, and the tailgate lower channel rot from the inside out; drain holes plug. A good used or repro tailgate is $600–$1,500 and often needs paint.', 'Windshield frame, cowl, and A-pillar corners: the windshield surround rusts under the gasket and leaks into the cowl and kick panels. Repair means glass out and welding — $1,500–$3,000 with glass and paint.', "Engines: the IH 304/345/392 V8s are torquey and durable but low-compression and thirsty (10–13 mpg). Common issues are cracked exhaust manifolds, hardened valve stem seals (blue smoke on startup), rear main seepage, and timing chain stretch past ~90k. Parts supply is aftermarket-dependent (IH Parts America, Super Scout Specialists, Scout Light Line); a full rebuild is $5,000–$8,000. Ask for a compression/leakdown record, not just 'runs great'.", 'Fuel system: the original Holley 2210/2300-series two-barrel is finicky and often replaced with a Motorcraft 2100 or Edelbrock. Original dual side-mounted fuel tanks rust, sending units fail, and the selector valve and steel lines corrode — expect $600–$1,500 to sort tanks, lines, pump, and sender. Sniff for gas smell in the cabin and under the rear.', "Cooling: 304 + TF727 combinations run hot in traffic; original radiators, fan clutches, and rotted heater cores are common. 'New radiator' is a good sign but confirm the fan clutch, shroud (often missing), water pump, and hoses were done as a system — $600–$1,200 for the rest.", 'Electrical: 40+ year old harnesses go brittle behind the dash and at the bulkhead/engine bay connectors; ammeter-based charging circuits, headlight switch, and turn-signal switch are common failure points and a real fire risk. Look for a documented harness replacement or at minimum clean, non-crispy, non-Scotch-locked wiring. Full harness $1,500–$3,000 installed. Points/Prestolite ignition is usually (and sensibly) converted to Pertronix or HEI.', 'Steering: Saginaw box wear, worn steering shaft rag joint, sagging Pitman/idler geometry and worn tie rod/drag link ends give the famous Scout wander. A rebuilt box plus full linkage rebuild is $1,200–$2,500 and transforms the truck. Also check the steering column mount and the frame-side box mounting area for cracks.', 'Brakes: front discs from 1974-on, drums prior; master cylinders, rubber flex lines, rear wheel cylinders, and the vacuum booster all age out. Sticky rear drums and a long pedal are typical. Full system refresh $1,200–$2,500. Confirm the parking brake actually works.', 'Drivetrain: the Chrysler TF727 automatic and T-19/T-428 four-speeds are stout; the Dana 20 transfer case leaks from the rear seal and gets sloppy shift detents. Dana 44 front (closed knuckle on early, later units too) and Dana 44/Dana 60 rear are strong, but front axle U-joints, knuckle seals, and wheel bearings are frequently overdue
profiles.immediate_repairs: Assume a full fluid and filter service (engine, TF727 with pan drop and filter, Dana 20, both diffs, brake fluid flush), all rubber brake flex lines plus a master cylinder, a carb rebuild or Motorcraft 2100 swap with fresh fuel filter and rubber lines, ignition tune (cap/rotor/wires/plugs or a Pertronix/HEI conversion), full steering linkage inspection with tie rod ends and rag joint as needed, new door/window/tailgate weatherstrip and a windshield gasket reseal, body mount bushing replacement, and battery/charging cleanup including the ammeter circuit. Budget $2,500–$5,000 at an independent shop, less if you do it yourself.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Expect a Saginaw steering box rebuild and possibly a steering shaft, front axle U-joints and knuckle/wheel bearing service, a cooling system round-out (water pump, fan clutch, shroud, heater core), exhaust from the manifolds back including cracked manifold repair, fuel tank and sender work, seat foam and interior trim, and localized rust repair on the rear quarters/floor once you know how deep the 'typical Scout rust' really goes. $4,000–$9,000 is realistic; a proper quarter-panel and floor job alone can eat all of it.
profiles.market_notes: Values are driven almost entirely by metal quality, documentation, and how honest the presentation is: a rust-free Arizona/California truck with the original line-setting ticket and receipts can be double a rusty one with identical mileage. Traveler and Terra long-wheelbase bodies and SSII/Rallye trim carry premiums, as do factory 345/392 V8s, four-speed manuals, factory A/C, and desirable two-tone paint; automatics are normal and not a penalty on a truck like this. Mileage matters far less than a documented engine/trans rebuild and evidence of professional rust repair. At $29k the market expects either a solid, well-documented driver or a truck with clearly disclosed and quantified rust — 'some typical Scout rust' with no photos is a price-negotiation lever, not a description.
profiles.catchup_notes: A 45-year-old Scout II that has not had a documented recommissioning needs the full age-related sweep regardless of mileage: all rubber (brake lines, fuel lines, coolant hoses, weatherstrip, body mounts, suspension bushings), the wiring harness assessed for brittleness, and every fluid changed. Assume $3,000–$6,000 of catch-up in year one on a good example, and treat any 'some typical rust' language as an open-ended line item until you have seen it on a lift.

profiles.label: Land Rover LR4 / Discovery 4 (L319, 2010–2016, incl. HSE Lux & Landmark)
profiles.framing: For this buyer the LR4 is a genuinely capable, seven-seat family and Central Coast adventure wagon: Terrain Response, twin-speed transfer case, air suspension and real ground clearance in a package that still rides like a luxury car on Highway 1. It is not an investment and should never be bought as one — final-year 2016 Landmark cars have a modest collector halo, but running costs behave like a used luxury SUV with a hand-built British electrical system. What matters is documentation of the expensive stuff (timing chain hardware on the AJ126 supercharged V6, coolant pipes, air suspension, differentials) and a car that has been serviced by a specialist rather than deferred. Buy the best-documented example, not the cheapest, and budget a real reserve from day one.
profiles.weak_points:
1) AJ126 3.0 supercharged V6 timing chain and tensioner wear (2014–2016 cars, and the related AJ133 5.0 V8 chain issue on 2010–2013): a cold-start rattle of 1–3 seconds, chain stretch codes (P0016/P0017/P0018), or a whirring/ticking at idle points to guides and hydraulic tensioners. Failure is catastrophic (valve-to-piston contact). Preventive chain service is engine-out or front-cover-off labor, roughly $6,000–$10,000 at an independent, more at a dealer. Ask for a cold-start video with sound and any chain/tensioner invoices; unrecorded 90k+ cars carry this risk unpriced.
2) Plastic coolant crossover pipes / thermostat housing / water pump on the 3.0 SC: the OEM composite pipes under the supercharger go brittle with heat cycles and can split without warning, dumping coolant and risking overheat damage to an aluminum engine. Aftermarket billet-aluminum pipe upgrade kits exist and are the tell of a knowledgeable owner; expect $1,200–$2,500 done with the water pump and thermostat while access is open. Look for a receipt naming 'coolant crossover pipes,' 'aluminum pipe upgrade,' or supercharger removal.
3) Supercharger nose-cone bearings and the isolator/coupler: a whine changing pitch or a rattle at idle around 80–120k miles. Nose cone rebuild $600–$1,200; whole blower far more.
4) Air suspension: EAS compressor (Hitachi/AMK) and dryer wear out around 80–130k miles, symptoms are slow rise, 'Suspension Fault' messages, a car that sits low overnight, or a compressor that runs long and hot. Compressor with dryer $600–$1,400 installed; individual air springs $350–$700 each; valve block and height sensors add up. Coil-spring conversions are a red flag on a car this buyer wants unmodified.
5) Cooling-system periphery generally: expansion tank cracks, radiator and intercooler-circuit auxiliary pump, and the low-temp radiator on SC cars. A one-time overheat event can cook the engine — check for coolant staining in the vee and Carfax/dealer notes of 'overheating.'
6) Rear differential and driveshaft: rear diff bearing whine and pinion seal leaks appear from ~90k; center support bearing and rear driveshaft U-joints/flex disc cause a 40–60 mph vibration or clunk on throttle transitions. Driveshaft $700–$1,400, rear diff rebuild/replace $1,800–$3,500.
7) Front suspension wear items: lower control arm bushings and ball joints, plus front upper arms — typical at 70–110k, causing a shimmy over the mid-corner ruts on local backroads. All four arms $1,200–$2,000; alignment mandatory after air-suspension or arm work.
8) Sunroof and body drains: the triple-sunroof cars (Landmark, HSE Lux) plug drains and wet the headliner, A-pillars and, worse, the passenger footwell and front SRS/BCM connectors — check for damp carpet padding and musty smell. Also alpine window seals and tailgate/upper-glass hinge corrosion.
9) Electrical gremlins and parasitic drain: a weak battery causes cascading warning lights (park brake, suspension, transmission fault). Electric parking brake actuator module failure ($700–$1,200), HVAC blend-door actuators, front and rear camera/infotainment modules, and door-latch/window regulator faults are common. Always test every module cold and hot.
10) In-tank fuel pump / low-pressure fuel supply failures on the SC V6 (this generation has documented pump replacements around 60–90k, ~$900–$1,600) plus high-pressure pump and injector issues showing as long crank or misfire under load.
11) Oil leaks: cam cover gaskets, oil cooler/filter housing, and the timing cover on high-mile motors — usually $500–$1,500 each depending on access; a soaked engine bay masks the more serious coolant leaks.
12) Transmission: the ZF 8HP is strong but was 'filled for life.' A 98k car with no fluid service should get a pan/filter/fluid change ($500–$800); look for shudder at light throttle 1,200–1,600 rpm (torque converter lock-up) and harsh 2-3 shifts.
13) Brakes and tires: heavy vehicle, front rotors/pads every 30–40k ($900–$1,400 axle set with rotors); 20
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up (engine oil, ZF 8HP pan/filter/fluid if undocumented, front/rear diff and transfer case fluid, brake fluid, coolant condition test); four matching tires if the set is mixed or aged; new AGM battery unless dated within ~3 years; air-suspension full-cycle test and likely compressor/dryer service; clear all stored fault codes and re-scan after a 100-mile shakedown; clean all four sunroof and A-pillar drains; front brake pads/rotors if under 4mm; correct any cam-cover or oil-cooler seepage. Expect $2,500–$5,000 on a typical 90–100k example.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Coolant crossover pipe upgrade with water pump and thermostat if not already documented ($1,200–$2,500); front lower control arm bushings/ball joints and alignment ($1,200–$2,000); air spring(s) or valve block as leaks appear ($400–$1,500); supercharger nose-cone bearing or isolator if whining ($600–$1,200); rear driveshaft center bearing/flex disc or rear diff seals ($700–$1,800); HVAC actuator, parking-brake module or camera/infotainment module repair ($400–$1,200); spark plugs and both drive belts if not stamped. Timing-chain service is the big contingency if any cold-start rattle or chain codes appear.
profiles.market_notes: Price is driven first by service documentation — a folder showing coolant pipes, chain hardware, air suspension and transmission service is worth several thousand dollars over an equal-mileage mystery car. Final-year 2016 cars, especially the Landmark and HSE Lux with three sunroofs, Meridian, surround cameras and the HD/heavy-duty package (full-size matching spare, locking rear diff), carry a premium; missing HD pack and mismatched 20" tires are cheapening details. Sub-80k-mile examples and desirable color combos (Santorini Black, Fuji White, Corris Grey over Ebony) bring the strongest money, while any Carfax damage entries, unrepaired suspension faults, or coil-spring conversions produce steep discounts. Regional bidding for these on BaT clusters $18k–$32k depending on miles and records, with hollow-market risk below $15k where the buyer inherits every deferred item.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 90–100k mile LR4 arrives with life-of-vehicle fluids never changed, an aging battery causing phantom faults, a tired air-suspension compressor and original coolant pipes. Plan on a comprehensive fluid and consumables catch-up plus air-suspension and cooling-system attention in the first year, and treat undocumented timing-chain hardware as an open $6k–$10k liability rather than a solved problem.

profiles.label: Lexus RX 350 (AL10, 3rd generation)
profiles.framing: This is the low-drama family/utility slot in the garage: a 2GR-powered, port-or-D4S V6 crossover with a properly engineered automatic, a quiet cabin, and a parts and service network that reaches everywhere. For a Carmel-based buyer it is a Highway 1 / Salinas run-around and airport hauler that should never be the reason a weekend gets cancelled. Nothing about it is engaging, so the entire buying case rests on documentation, condition, and price relative to a market that stubbornly refuses to depreciate. Note that US-market 2010–2015 cars are the true AL10 with the 2GR-FE and U660E/U760E; 2016 is the AL20 redesign with the 2GR-FKS and 8-speed — mechanically similar in spirit but a different platform, so verify which car you are actually looking at.
profiles.weak_points: 1) Timing-cover and cam-tower oil seepage on the 2GR-FE is the signature 100k+ issue: the RTV-sealed front cover weeps down the back of the block and onto the subframe, often mistaken for a rear main leak. Diagnosis is easy from below with a light; repair is engine-out-of-the-way labor at roughly $1,800–3,000 at an independent. Ask for photos of a clean underside or a documented reseal. 2) Water pump failure/weeping around 80k–130k, usually announced by pink crust at the weep hole or a faint coolant smell; $500–900 including the belt. 3) The VVT-i oil supply line failure that killed early 2GR engines was addressed by recall/updated hard line on earlier cars, but on any 2GR verify the metal line is present and dry — a burst line dumps oil in seconds and destroys the engine. 4) U660E/U760E 6-speed: Lexus calls the WS fluid 'lifetime,' which it is not. Neglected units develop a 1-2 shift flare, torque-converter shudder at light throttle 35–50 mph, or a delayed engagement clunk. Drain-and-fills every 60k are cheap insurance; a car at 120k with zero fluid history is a $3,500–5,000 gamble. 2013+ F Sport uses the 8-speed U880E, which is fine but has its own valve-body software updates. 5) Melting/sticky and cracking dashboards on 2010–2013 cars, especially sun-belt and coastal-sun examples — Lexus ran a warranty extension that has now expired; replacement is $1,400–2,500. Check the top pad and the passenger airbag seam. 6) HVAC blend-door and mode actuators tick or knock behind the dash and cause split hot/cold; $250–600 each depending on access. 7) Remote Touch mouse controller and the 8-inch nav screen: sticky/erratic cursor, ghost touches, screen delamination or DVD/HDD nav drive failure. New OEM units are $900–1,800; many owners live with it or fit an aftermarket head unit (a modification this buyer should be wary of, as it often means hacked wiring). 8) Power liftgate struts and the electric lift actuator/motor fail around 100k — the gate drops, beeps, or refuses to latch; struts are cheap, the actuator is $600–1,000. 9) Suspension: front lower control arm bushings, sway bar end links, and strut mounts produce a clunk over Carmel Valley pavement joints by 100k–120k; struts and mounts all around run $1,200–2,000. Rear wheel bearings hum from ~120k, $400–600 each. 10) Hydraulic engine and transmission mounts collapse and cause a diesel-like idle shake in Drive; front mount $350–650 installed. 11) Spark plugs are a 120k service and the rear bank requires intake plenum removal — budget $450–700, not $120. 12) A/C condenser stone damage and slow leaks are common on freeway cars; condenser plus recharge $700–1,100. Also check for the compressor clutch rattle at idle. 13) AWD models: the transfer case and rear diff fluids are almost never changed, and the driveshaft center support bearing rumbles at 40–60 mph on higher-mileage cars. 14) Sunroof drains clog with coastal pine needles and Monterey litter, soaking the A-pillar trim and headliner — pull the trim and look for water staining, plus check the spare well for standing water.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Full fluid catch-up: transmission WS drain-and-fill (repeat in 500 miles if the old fluid is dark), coolant if past 10 years, brake fluid flush, transfer case and rear diff on AWD. Four new tires if the DOT codes are over six years old regardless of tread (very common on low-mile Lexus SUVs), plus an alignment. New 12V battery if undated or over four years, cabin and engine air filters, wiper blades, and a sunroof-drain flush. Expect to fix at least one HVAC actuator tick or a pair of liftgate struts. Budget $1,500–2,800.
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if not documented; timing-cover reseal if seepage is dripping rather than weeping; spark plugs and coil inspection at 120k; front strut assemblies and sway bar links if it clunks; engine and transmission mounts if it shakes at idle in Drive; a rear wheel bearing; brake pads and rotors all around; possibly a dash pad replacement on a 2010–2013 sun-baked car. Budget $2,000–4,000.
profiles.market_notes: RX 350s trade on records and mileage bands more than on spec — a one-owner car with a full Lexus dealer history and under 90k will command a real premium over an identical 120k trade-in. AWD carries a modest premium nationally but matters little on the Monterey Peninsula, so FWD is the value play; Navigation/Premium/Luxury packages, ventilated seats, blind-spot monitor, and the 2013+ F Sport add appeal, while the F Sport's stiffer ride and 19s add nothing for this mission. Neutral colors (Nebula Gray, Starfire Pearl, silver) with tan or black leather sell fastest; a clean, unmodified California car with no rust, no accidents, and a factory head unit is worth paying up for because the whole point of this vehicle is not thinking about it.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-15 year old RX arrives with 'lifetime' fluids that were never changed, original coolant, aging suspension bushings, and six-to-eight-year-old tires on a low-mile example. Plan on a full fluids-and-rubber reset in the first month — trans, coolant, brake fluid, diff/transfer case, tires, battery, belt — then treat water pump, spark plugs, and struts as scheduled 12-month items rather than surprises.

profiles.label: Porsche Boxster (981, incl. S / GTS / Spyder)
profiles.framing: The 981 is the sweet spot of modern Boxsters: the last naturally aspirated flat-six mid-engine Porsche roadster, with electric steering that is still genuinely good, a stiff aluminum-intensive chassis, and no IMS bearing to worry about. For a Carmel-based driver this is a near-ideal Highway 1 / Laureles Grade weekend car that can also be driven daily in the region's mild climate, with the caveat that it is a two-seat convertible with two small trunks. What matters here is a documented, unmodified-or-reversible example with a full Porsche/independent service file, a healthy convertible top mechanism, and evidence the engine has never been abused or run low on oil; the 9A1 flat-six is a strong motor but a bad one is a five-figure problem.
profiles.weak_points: ['Bore scoring / cylinder scuffing on the 9A1 DFI flat-six is uncommon but not extinct, and it is the single catastrophic risk. Symptoms are ticking or knocking at cold start that fades as it warms, oil consumption worse than roughly 1 qt / 1,200 miles, and a faint sooty smell. It shows up most often on hard-driven or short-tripped cars past 60-80k miles. A borescope of all six cylinders plus a DME over-rev report is the only real protection; an engine replacement or rebuild is $18,000-$28,000+.', 'Cracked cylinder heads / coolant loss on early 9A1 engines (mostly 2013-2014) present as slow, unexplained coolant level drop with no visible external leak, sometimes with a sweet smell after a hard drive. Head or engine work is $8,000-$20,000.', 'Water pump with a composite impeller typically fails between 60k and 100k miles or roughly 8-10 years; symptoms are weeping from the pump area, coolant smell, or temperature creep in traffic. Budget $1,100-$1,800 done properly with a thermostat and coolant service. On a 78k-mile 2014 with no pump record, assume it is due.', 'Coolant expansion tank and its cap crack with age, and the plastic coolant hard lines / hose connectors get brittle. Look for dried pink-orange crust in the engine bay and at the rear of the block. $400-$900.', 'Air-oil separator (AOS) diaphragm failure causes a big puff of blue smoke at startup or after a highway pull, rough idle, and oil consumption. Typical at 70k-100k miles; $700-$1,200 installed. Frequently misdiagnosed as bore scoring, so a proper crankcase vacuum test is worth insisting on.', 'Rear main seal and, less often, the case-half seam weep oil onto the transaxle bellhousing. A light film is common; drips that require topping off mean pulling the transaxle, which is a $2,000-$3,500 job unless combined with a clutch.', 'Manual cars: dual-mass flywheel and clutch. Judder from a stop, high engagement point, or a rattle at idle that disappears with the clutch depressed means DMF. Replacement with flywheel and rear main seal while you are in there runs $3,000-$4,500. Most 981 manuals go 80k-120k miles, so a 78k car is inside the window.', 'PDK cars: the 60k-mile / 6-year mechatronic fluid and filter service is $700-$1,100 and is skipped constantly. Cable or hydraulic repairs run $1,200-$2,500; a full top replacement is $2,800-$4,500. profiles.market_notes: Transmission and engine drive the money: a 6-speed manual commands a clear premium over PDK in the enthusiast market, and Boxster S / GTS 3.4 cars trade several thousand above a 2.7 base regardless of options. Spec matters at the margins - Sport Chrono with PSE, adaptive sport seats, PASM, a non-black interior, and a genuinely interesting exterior color lift a car; base cloth-spec silver/white/black cars with 19s and no options sit. Records are worth real money on this generation: a folder showing water pump, PDK or clutch service, brake fluid history, and no accidents will beat a lower-mileage undocumented car with a damage entry. Aftermarket exhaust, non-N-spec tires, and a Carfax damage report each shave value, and mileage bands break roughly at 40k, 70k, and 100k.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 10-12 year old, 70-80k mile 981 needs a deferred-maintenance sweep even when it looks perfect: brake fluid, coolant, plugs and coils, AGM battery with coding, water pump if undocumented, N-spec tires, and a convertible top lubrication and drain cleanout. Coastal Monterey cars additionally want the front duct liners pulled to clean debris off the radiators and condensers before corrosion sets in. Plan $3,000-$5,000 of catch-up in the first year on top of the purchase price, separate from the clutch/DMF or PDK service that lurks in the next 20k miles.

profiles.label: Porsche Cayman / Cayman S (987.2, DFI)
profiles.framing: The 987.2 is the sweet spot of the mid-engine Porsche line for a real-world driver: the 2009+ DFI engines (2.9 base, 3.4 S) shed the M96/M97 IMS bearing and bore-scoring anxiety that haunts the 987.1, and the chassis is still small, light, hydraulically steered, and immensely usable. For this buyer it is a Monterey Peninsula weekend and errand car that can also take Highway 1 or a canyon run without drama, and can absorb a real road trip with front and rear trunks. What matters most is documented maintenance from a Porsche specialist, an unmolested drivetrain and suspension, no track history, and a clean, complete car rather than the cheapest example. Options and transmission matter enormously to resale here — a well-optioned manual S in a real color is a different asset than a base-spec PDK.
profiles.weak_points: Water pump and thermostat: plastic impeller pumps are a consumable, typically 60k–90k miles or 8–10 years; symptoms are weeping from the pump vent hole, pink crust on the block, or slow warm-up. Budget $900–$1,600 installed; look for a receipt in the last ~60k. Coolant expansion tank and its cap crack with age — cheap parts, but a low-coolant light or crusty residue at the tank seam signals neglect. Radiators and A/C condensers sit low in the front bumper and pack with leaves and debris; corrosion-through causes coolant loss and the front radiator ducts trap moisture. Ask for photos of the front radiator area with the ducts removed and check for the debris-screen retrofit; a pair of radiators plus condensers is $1,800–$3,000. Rear main seal and AOS: the DFI engines are far better than 987.1 but still weep; a smoky cold-start plume or oil at the bellhousing means AOS ($700–$1,200) or RMS/clutch-out job ($2,000–$3,500 on a manual, more if the PDK must come out). Coil packs and DFI high-pressure fuel system: coil failure causes misfire codes and rough idle, cheap to fix; the high-pressure fuel pump and DFI injectors are the expensive tail — injector or HPFP work runs $1,200–$2,500. Carbon buildup on intake valves is inherent to direct injection; by 80k–100k expect mild hesitation and rough cold idle, walnut blasting $900–$1,500. PDK: the 7-speed dual-clutch is robust but requires fluid and filter service every ~40k miles at $700–$1,000; a neglected PDK with juddering low-speed engagement or delayed 1–2 shifts is a mechatronic/clutch-pack risk of $4,000–$9,000+. Demand a dated PDK service invoice, not a seller's recollection. Manual cars: dual-mass flywheel and clutch typically 60k–100k; a rattling clutch pedal at idle or high engagement point means $2,500–$3,500 with an RMS and IMS-free rear-end reseal. Suspension bushings and control arms: by 80k the rear toe links, front lower control arm bushings and top mounts are tired — squeaks over expansion joints, wandering alignment; a full round of arms and an alignment is $1,800–$3,500. Coilover conversions (Bilstein PSS9/PSS10) on an old car usually mean worn shock seals and a track past; PASM cars with a leaking OE damper are $1,000+ each. Rear decklid spoiler mechanism jams or throws a fault; motor/mechanism $600–$1,200. Ignition switch and the alarm/immobilizer module, plus the door-lock actuators and the microswitches in the doors, cause phantom drains and no-crank conditions; a parasitic draw complaint deserves investigation. Interior: soft-touch coating on the center console, glovebox and door pulls turns sticky with sun exposure; the Sport Chrono stopwatch bezel and the cupholder arms break. Bore scoring is largely a 987.1 issue but a borescope of all six cylinders and a leakdown are still the right money on any 15-year-old flat six. Finally, aftermarket high-flow cats: they routinely set P0420/P0430 and are not California-legal — a CEL from cats is a smog and registration problem in Carmel, not a cosmetic annoyance, and OE manifolds/cats to restore are $2,000–$4,000.
profiles.immediate_repairs: Fluids and filters if not documented within a year (engine oil, brake fluid on a 2-year cycle, coolant condition check). PDK fluid and filter service if there is no dated invoice within 40k miles. Full four-wheel alignment, especially on a coilover-equipped car. Tires: verify DOT dates — anything over 6 years old gets replaced regardless of tread, and mismatched front/rear brands (Michelin front, Continental rear as in the example) should be corrected to a matched staggered set, ~$1,400–$2,000. Brake pads and rotors if Hawk HP Plus track pads are fitted; those are unusable on the street (noise, cold bite) — swap to OE-spec pads and rotors, $1,200–$1,800. Diagnose and resolve any CEL: on a California-registered car, aftermarket cats setting P0420/P0430 must be addressed to pass smog, likely
profiles.repairs_12mo: Water pump and thermostat if not already replaced. Radiators and condensers if the front-end inspection shows corrosion or fin damage. Walnut-blast carbon cleaning and new spark plugs/coils at 90k–100k. Rear suspension bushings, toe links and drop links; front lower control arms if bushings are cracked. AOS if any cold-start smoke appears. Clutch and DMF on a manual approaching 90k. Serpentine belt, brake fluid flush, and a second oil service. Convertible-top items do not apply, but the rear spoiler mechanism and door-lock actuators are common one-off $600–$1,200 hits. Interior soft-touch trim refinishing if the sticky-coating problem is present.
profiles.market_notes: Manual transmission commands a meaningful premium over PDK on 987.2 Caymans and that gap has widened; PDK cars are the value play but sell slower. The S (3.4 DFI, 320 hp) is worth clearly more than the 2.9 base, and the Cayman R is a separate, much higher tier. Color and options drive the top of the market: PCCB-free but well-optioned cars in Guards Red, GT Silver, Aqua Blue, Peridot, or any PTS/special color with Sport Chrono, PASM, LSD, sport seats and full leather bring the money, while Arctic Silver over black is the most common and least differentiated combination. Documented Porsche-dealer or independent-specialist service history, a fresh PDK service, and a clean unmodified state are worth thousands; aftermarket cats, coilovers, harness bars and a CEL suggest track use and push a car firmly into the discount tier — realistically 15–25% under a stock, documented equivalent. Mileage bands matter less than records; 60k–90k with a binder beats 45k with a shrug.
profiles.catchup_notes: A typical 80k-mile 987.2 is now 15 years old and due for a full round of rubber and cooling: water pump/thermostat, coolant flush, expansion tank cap, radiator cleanout with debris screens, suspension bushings and toe links, and a fresh matched set of tires regardless of tread depth. DFI carbon cleaning and plugs land around 90k-100k. Plan roughly $4,000-$7,000 of catch-up in the first two years even on a well-kept car, and add the cost of restoring compliant catalytic converters if the car will be registered in California.

For a 126k-mile 1UR-FE truck whose two big-ticket risks (secondary air injection, KDSS) are both diagnostic questions, this is thin.

condition.rationale: The visible car presents well: straight silver bodywork, clean bronze Method wheels with a matched set of deep-tread KO3s, GOBI rack fitted squarely, no obvious damage in the two photos that are actually this vehicle. Brand-new ICON suspension and a rear brake job (claimed) address two normal wear areas. But 126k miles with no evidence on air-injection codes, KDSS lean, valley-plate/timing-cover seepage, transfer-case actuator, or original bushings/ball joints leaves the expensive half of the car unexamined, and the fresh lift can mask worn steering and driveline components on a short test drive.

price_value.rationale: $31,995 for a 126k-mile base-trim 2014 is out of line with the buyer's own comps: a 63.5k-mile 2013 Convenience AWD asks $25,040 in Palm Desert and a 128.5k-mile 2017 Premium asks $23,900; a 142.9k-mile 2010 sold for $14,250. The dealer's own board shows a 124k-mile 2014 at $29,995 and a 147k-mile 2015 at $27,995, so this unit is priced at the top of its own lot. The premium is entirely the ICON/GOBI/ARB build, which is dealer-installed cost that does not return at resale, and the asking price alone exceeds Jason's $27,000 max before tax, registration, or any catch-up work — all-in lands near the $33,000 defeats-purpose line.

mission_fit.rationale: As capability, this is genuinely what the RX 350 cannot do: body-on-frame, full-time 4WD with locking center diff, 285/70R17 A/Ts, roof rack and awning for dogs, gear and light camping — the mission brief's exact target. But it is also a second big Lexus SUV, and the catch-up note warns of RX overlap; it justifies itself only on off-road/overland character. Paying a modified-truck premium to add that character, while the BMW replacement budget is what is actually under pressure, weakens the fit rather than the concept.

logistics.rationale: San Diego is roughly 455 miles from Carmel — a comfortable fly-or-drive day, and a good car drives itself home on new tires. emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Silver over black leather with bronze Method wheels, a GOBI stealth rack and an ARB awning is a coherent, tasteful overland look, and ICON is quality hardware rather than a cheap spacer lift. It has real character and would be a pleasant, torquey, quiet thing to own. Logistics are the strong point: 455 in-state miles, a storefront dealer who must supply smog, and a straightforward PPI at a San Diego specialist. Mission-wise it delivers real capability the RX 350 lacks, but it is a second big Lexus SUV purchased at the top of its market while the 335i replacement budget is the actual constraint. Worth a scan-and-receipts conversation; not worth $31,995.

But this is a base/Convenience car, not a Premium or Luxury, it carries a damage report and an undiagnosed dash/temperature complaint, and it sits close to the $27,000 maximum price with the 13-year fluid catch-up still ahead of it. Private-party at retail money with open questions is fair, not a bargain.

mission_fit.rationale: As the utility_capability branch this does supply what the RX 350 cannot: body-on-frame construction, full-time 4WD with low range, a factory tow package, 6,500 lb capability, a third row and factory roof rails suitable for a rooftop tent or platform sleeping. Against that, it is a second large luxury SUV in a two-car household that already has one, it consumes most of the price ceiling, and it does nothing for the enthusiast-bridge brief the 335i's retirement actually creates. It is a capability purchase, not the manual bridge car.

logistics.rationale: Palm Desert is a straightforward drive or short flight from Carmel and an easy car to drive home. PPI access should be excellent: the vehicle is a known quantity at four Southern California Lexus dealers, the seller proposes closing at a certified Lexus dealership, and an independent Toyota/Lexus specialist inspection near Palm Desert is easy to arrange. California title and registration, emissions passed in 2022, 2024 and 2025, so smog is procedurally routine — the seller must still supply a current certificate.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Silver over charcoal, base trim with the Convenience Package, automatic, running boards and chrome — a competent, anonymous family hauler rather than anything with character. No off-road package, no interesting colour, no manual, and it is closer to the RX in feel than to the Z3, GTI or MINI he actually wants. It earns its keep only as capability.
