ppi_focus: Cooling system: pressure test cold and hot, inspect valley plate and timing-cover area for seepage, check coolant condition and level, watch the temperature gauge on a loaded uphill drive replicating the reported symptom.

Full OBD-II scan for stored, pending and permanent codes with readiness monitors, specifically P2440/P2442 secondary air injection; also check charging system and battery condition given the reported light flicker.

Front-end collision check: radiator support, bumper reinforcement, headlight tabs, park-assist sensor function, panel gap and paint-depth readings across the nose after the July 2026 bumper replacement.

Rear suspension: verify rear shock installation and hardware torque, listen for the reported metal-to-metal ping over bumps and on turns, check subframe and control-arm bushings and the panhard rod after the pothole impact.
Front struts fitted Jan 2026 — confirm OEM parts, correct install, and that the 12-month Lexus warranty is transferable; recheck alignment and front tire inside-edge wear.
Frame and underbody corrosion survey with the car on a lift, given Alaska titling 2015–2022; probe rails, crossmembers, brake and fuel lines, and shock mounts.
Confirm KDSS presence; if fitted, check accumulator, valve body and lines for weeping and measure cross-vehicle ride height for lean.
Transfer case and 4WD function: engage low range, check actuator operation, inspect transfer case and differential fluids for condition and level; verify no seep at output seals.
Tires: record brand, model and DOT date codes on all five, check for mixed sizes or tread depths that would strain the full-time 4WD driveline.
Verify instrument cluster part number against the VIN build and cross-check the odometer against the 08/08/2026 Lexus record of 63,363–63,370 miles.
what_would_change_verdict: A dated Lexus or independent specialist report clearing the 08/07/2026 temperature-gauge and light-flicker complaint, plus a clean cooling-system pressure test and a scan with no stored or permanent codes, would move this up materially.

A body shop invoice and pre-repair photos showing the July 2026 damage was a cosmetic front bumper strike only, with no radiator-support or structural involvement, would neutralise the biggest documentation conflict.

A lift inspection confirming no frame corrosion after the Alaska years, correct rear shock installation with no noise, and a matched set of tires with recent date codes would support the asking price.
Evidence of a recurring or unexplained temperature/electrical fault, frame corrosion, or a P2440/P2442 code would drop this below consideration at this money.
A negotiated price meaningfully below the $25,040 ask — reflecting the damage report, the twice-done rear brakes and the outstanding 13-year fluid catch-up — would improve the risk-adjusted value.
evidence.mission_note: As the utility_capability branch this does deliver what the RX 350 cannot — body-on-frame, low range, tow package, third row and factory roof rails for a rooftop tent or sleeping platform — so it is not merely a second RX. But it is a capability purchase that consumes most of the price ceiling while leaving the enthusiast-bridge need created by the 335i entirely unsolved, so it should be judged strictly as a pragmatic capability buy and only bought if the open temperature-gauge and damage questions close cleanly.
evidence.rationale: This is the best-documented private listing in the set and simultaneously the one with the most unresolved recent history. The Carfax and Lexus repair-order printout verify 63,363 miles with no rollback indication, a guaranteed clean California title, three owners, all recalls performed, and a genuine recent spend at Lexus dealers: both front struts (Jan 2026, found blown at 61k), both rear shocks (Jul 2026), front brakes (Aug 2025) and rear brakes twice (Feb and Jul 2026). Against that, the documents contradict the listing's 'No Accident or Damage Reported' banner — Carfax shows minor damage on 07/24/2026 and the 07/16/2026 order shows a sublet front bumper replacement the seller advertises as a feature. More seriously, the Lexus Escondido order of 08/07/2026 records the owner reporting a temperature gauge swinging hot and cold with dash lights flickering on inclines, and declining any diagnostic; on a 1UR-FE whose known weak points are valley-plate coolant leaks and secondary air injection, with no coolant service documented in thirteen years, that symptom is exactly the thing that cannot be left unexamined. The August 2025 pothole, the twice-repeated rear brake job, the owner's own cluster-tampering question that Lexus could not resolve, and a Bureau of Automotive Repair case all form a cluster of activity in the month before the car was listed. Price at $25,040 tracks the $24,420 Carfax value and is fair for a low-mile California car, but it is a base/Convenience trim, it sits close to the $27,000 maximum, and the fluid catch-up plus the diagnostic work are still ahead. Logistics are the strongest part of the picture: Palm Desert is an easy trip, the car is well known to four Lexus dealers, and the seller proposes closing at a dealership, so a genuine PPI is realistic. Contingent interest, not a buy at the ask until the temperature-gauge complaint and the damage event are documented closed.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller for the body-shop invoice and pre-repair photos behind the 07/24/2026 damage report, and book a pre-purchase inspection at an independent Toyota/Lexus specialist near Palm Desert with an explicit brief to pressure-test the cooling system, scan for permanent/history codes including P2440/P2442, and lift-inspect the frame — before discussing price.

VIN decodes 1.8L; listing describes a 2.0L over-bored replacement M42. This is explained by the documented engine swap/over-bore, not an identity problem, but the registered/insured engine spec should be confirmed.

critical_evidence.evidence: Not applicable in the M20 sense: the M42 is chain-driven. The listing states a 'replacement timing set' was installed with the 2022 engine build; no invoice reproduced, and the M42 upper chain guide/tensioner is its own known wear item.

One underbody photo of the rear differential/subframe area shows clean, freshly finished components with only light surface rust on the diff cover; no shock-tower, trunk battery corner, floor pan, jack point or rocker photos provided. Canadian-market car of unknown pre-2016 climate exposure.

Carfax records an October 2008 moderate front-damage accident and an April 2009 damage claim; the listing acknowledges hood and front fender repaint but provides no repair invoices, no radiator support / frame rail / apron photos and no paint depth readings.

No overheating history, coolant-system refresh record, compression/leakdown numbers, or Haltech temperature/AFR logs are provided for the 2022-built engine; head was 'reportedly' ported and polished with no machine-shop paperwork shown.

documentation.rationale: Real strengths: published VIN, Carfax with 8 service and 44 detailed records, owner's manuals, a photographed records folder, build-bench photos of the forged rotating assembly, and a named tuning shop. But every substantive claim about the build, the clutch, the LSD and the A/C rebuild is 'reportedly/said to be' in listing prose; no invoices, dyno sheet, machine-shop paperwork, compression numbers or 2008 accident repair documentation are reproduced. Long single ownership through the build helps, but for a car whose value rests entirely on build quality, the verifiable layer is thin.

condition.rationale: Presentation is genuinely strong: straight silver panels with even reflections, tidy shutlines, intact sport seat bolsters, an uncracked dash top, and an engine bay that looks assembled with care. Recent hardware is dated and plausible — 2026 brake overhaul (master, calipers, rotors, pads), 2026 tires, 2024 subframe/control arms/wheel bearings, 2024 driveshaft center bearing and CV boots. The single underbody photo is clean and dry. What pulls it down is what is not shown: no shock tower, trunk battery corner or floor photos on a Canadian-market car, no health data on a 2022 built engine (leakdown, coolant temps, oil pressure log), and a documented front-end collision whose inner structure has never been photographed.

price_value.rationale: At the captured $3,600 opening bid it looks cheap, but this is a reserve auction with 258 watchers and a build story; realistic hammer is well into the mid-to-high teens plus 5% buyer fee, which lands above Jason's $15k all-in bridge target and near his ideal band ceiling. Against the peer 1987 325is at $11,000, this is a four-cylinder 318is with a Carfax moderate accident, repainted front clip, a bespoke standalone-managed engine and non-CARB hardware — exactly the profile that the documentation-driven E30 market discounts on resale. You would be paying enthusiast-build money for an asset whose next buyer pool is narrow.

mission_fit.rationale: It clears the manual requirement and it is local and inspectable, but the mission asks for a reliable, easy-to-resell, sub-$15k-all-in bridge with low ownership friction. A 10.5:1 forged M42 on ITBs and a Haltech tune, with a cat-delete pipe and CARB-questionable hardware in a state where Jason must smog it every two years, is the opposite of low friction — and his mechanic does VW/Toyota, not standalone tuning. Resale in 6-24 months depends on finding another E30 build buyer rather than the broad market.

logistics.rationale: San Mateo is roughly 85 miles from Carmel — a same-day drive for a PPI and a drive home. Seller is a private party, publicly responsive, offering additional photos, videos and records, plus a new catalytic converter, the stock airboxes and a current passing California smog certificate to a California buyer. California title in his name, no transport needed. The only logistics friction is the auction clock (closes 2026-09-11) which compresses PPI scheduling.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Sterling Silver over black leatherette, sport seats, sunroof, Alpina-style 16s, M-Technic wheel, LSD and a short shifter is a handsome, coherent E30 coupe that would be a genuine Carmel Valley Road car, and the ITB noise is a real draw. It falls short of the profile's ideal on two counts: it is a 318is four rather than the M20 325is six the buyer's brief describes, and it is a heavily modified car rather than a preserved, documented original — the character is the builder's, not the factory's.

known_work_items: Catalyst-delete pipe currently fitted — install catalytic converter and restore a smog-legal exhaust configuration for California registration (seller supplies a new cat; labor and any re-tune remain)
CARB compliance of Haltech standalone ECU and Dbilas ITBs unresolved — potential BAR referee visit and/or reinstallation of the included stock intake/airbox/ECU with re-tune
positives: 85 miles from Carmel with a cooperative private seller who publicly offers extra photos, videos, records, a new catalytic converter, the stock intake hardware and a current passing California smog certificate — PPI and pickup are trivially easy.
Genuine manual E30 coupe with 325is LSD, sport seats, short shifter and an uncracked dash; photos show straight silver panels, clean shutlines and a tidy, unmolested-looking interior.

Substantial recent dated chassis work: 2026 brake overhaul (master cylinder, calipers, rotors, pads, lines), 2026 tires, 2024 325 rear subframe/control arms/wheel bearings, 2024 driveshaft center support and CV boots.
Long, transparent single ownership since 2017 with the whole build executed under that owner, plus Carfax showing 8 service and 44 detailed records and owner's manuals included.
Underbody photo of the rear end shows dry, freshly finished subframe and diff area with no visible structural corrosion in that region.
Included spare parts (stock ITB alternative manifold, airboxes, factory ECU, valve springs, mats) meaningfully reduce the cost of reversing the car toward compliance or stock.
concerns: Observed: Carfax shows an October 2008 accident with moderate front damage plus an April 2009 damage claim, and the hood and front fenders were repainted — no repair invoices, no radiator support/frame rail/apron photos, no paint readings are offered.

Observed: the car runs a catalyst-delete pipe, a Haltech standalone ECU and ITBs, was flagged a California Gross Polluter in 2021, and the listing itself concedes the mods 'may not be CARB-certified' — biennial smog for a Carmel-registered car is an open liability despite the seller's certificate offer.

Observed: a 10.5:1 forged, ported, standalone-tuned M42 is a specialist asset — Jason's VW/Toyota mechanic cannot support it, and the resale pool in 6-24 months is E30 build buyers, not the documentation-driven market that pays the strong money.
Observed: Toyo Proxes R888R semi-slicks are a track compound — marginal in Highway 1 wet and cold, and they will wear out fast in normal use even though they are new.

Unverified: no health evidence for the 2022-built engine — no leakdown/compression, oil pressure or Haltech coolant-temp/AFR logs, and no machine-shop paperwork for the ported head (ask for a datalog, leakdown sheet and the build invoices).
Unverified: this is a Canadian-market car with unknown pre-2016 climate exposure and no shock-tower, trunk battery corner, floor or rocker photos (ask for lift photos of those specific areas).
unknowns: Inner structural condition behind the repainted front clip after the 2008 moderate-damage accident (rad support, frame rails, aprons, fender seams).

seller_questions: Can you post the actual invoices for the 2022 engine build — machine shop, JE pistons, H-beam rods, VAC springs, head port work — with dates and the engine mileage since assembly?
What is the current leakdown or compression reading on all four cylinders, and can you provide a dated printout or a video of the test?
Can you export and post a Haltech datalog from a 20-minute drive showing coolant temp, oil pressure, AFR and any knock/limp events?
In exactly what configuration was the December 2024 smog certificate obtained — cat installed, stock airbox, and which ECU was in the car at the time?
Has this car ever been through a BAR referee inspection with the Haltech and ITBs, and if so can you post the certificate?
Do you have any invoices, photos or an insurance estimate from the 2008 front-end repair, and can you post lift photos of the radiator support, frame rails and inner fender aprons?
Can you post lift photos of the front shock towers under the strut hats, the trunk battery-tray corner, the floor pans, rockers and jack points?
What is the engine's coolant temperature after 20 minutes of Highway 1 driving and at idle in traffic, and has the radiator, expansion tank or thermostat been replaced since the build?
Has the M42 profile gasket ever been replaced, and is there any oil/coolant intermixing or weeping at the block/head seam?
Is the shown 122k km original to the chassis — do you have the Canadian export paperwork and the pre-2016 service history?
Will you allow a pre-purchase inspection at an independent BMW specialist of my choosing in the Bay Area before the auction closes, and can you deliver the car there?
What is included with the promised smog certificate — will the new catalytic converter be installed and the tune adjusted for it before delivery, or is that the buyer's job?
ppi_focus: Cylinder leakdown and compression on the built M42, plus cold-start behaviour and oil pressure at hot idle.
Cooling system pressure test and inspection of the M42 profile-gasket seam, radiator, expansion tank and hoses for weeping or intermixing.
Structural check of the repaired front end: paint depth on hood/fenders, radiator support and frame rail alignment, weld and sealant originality behind the fenders.
Rust survey specific to a Canadian car: front shock towers under the strut hats, trunk battery corner, rear subframe and trailing-arm mounting points, floors, jack points, sunroof drains.
Haltech scan and datalog review — fault history, AFR under load, coolant temp, and whether the tune tolerates a catalytic converter and the stock airbox.
Chase Bays braided brake and power-steering line installation quality and DOT-compliance of the fittings, plus master cylinder and pedal feel after the 2026 overhaul.
Drivetrain: 325is LSD lock-up test (one-wheel spin), diff and output seal leaks, driveshaft center bearing vibration at 45-60 mph, clutch engagement and any throwout squeal.
Suspension and steering after the E36 M3 rack conversion: alignment printout, bump steer, poly bushing NVH, ball joints, tie rods and Bilstein damper condition.
Electrical: instrument cluster odometer/OBC operation on the km cluster, A/C output temperature after the claimed rebuild, sunroof operation, LED headlight beam pattern legality.
Emissions dry-run: confirm the car can be presented smog-legal with the supplied cat and stock intake, ideally by taking it to a smog shop as part of the PPI.
what_would_change_verdict: Full build invoices plus a clean leakdown and a Haltech datalog showing normal coolant temps and AFR, combined with lift photos or a specialist PPI confirming no structural damage from the 2008 front hit and no rust — that would move it from a speculative build to a documented one.
A BAR referee certificate (or a smog certificate obtained in the exact configuration the car will be delivered in) that makes California registration a non-issue rather than an open liability.
A hammer price that keeps all-in under about $13,000 including fee and the compliance work — at that number the risk is priced in and it becomes a defensible fun bridge.
Bidding past roughly $16,000 all-in, or a PPI finding poor front-end repair, coolant-temp problems on the built motor, or shock-tower/subframe corrosion — any of those should end it.
Seller declining or slow-walking a pre-auction PPI at an independent Bay Area BMW specialist would make this a pass on principle.
evidence.mission_note: As an enthusiast bridge this is charismatic and geographically ideal but mission-adverse: a forged, standalone-tuned, cat-deleted 318is is a specialist toy that Jason's VW/Toyota mechanic cannot support, that carries an unresolved California emissions question, and that resells to a narrow build-buyer audience rather than quickly. It is not a pragmatic bridge either — the whole point of the bridge is dependable, cheap, easy-to-exit, and this car is none of those three despite looking the part.
evidence.rationale: This is a well-presented, heavily engineered E30 that fails the brief for structural reasons rather than cosmetic ones. The verifiable evidence is decent for a private BaT car — published VIN, Carfax with 8 service and 44 detailed records, build-bench photos, a named tuner, nine years of single ownership, and dated recent work (2026 brakes and tires, 2024 subframe, control arms, wheel bearings, driveshaft center bearing, CV boots) — but the entire value proposition, the 2022 forged 2.0L M42 with Haltech and ITBs, is supported only by seller prose: no invoices, no leakdown, no logs, no machine-shop paperwork. Carfax records an October 2008 moderate front-damage accident and a 2009 damage claim, the hood and front fenders are repainted, and no inner-structure photos or repair documentation exist. The car was a California Gross Polluter in 2021 and currently runs a catalyst-delete pipe with hardware the listing itself admits may not be CARB-certified, which sits in direct tension with the seller's promise of a passing smog certificate. It is a Canadian-market import with no shock-tower, trunk-corner or floor photos, so rust is unknown, not absent. Logistics are excellent — San Mateo, cooperative seller, easy PPI — and the emotional pull is real, but a reserve auction with 258 watchers points to a mid-to-high-teens hammer plus fee, above the sub-$15k all-in bridge target, for an asset that is harder to resell and harder to service than the GTI, F56 or 128i alternatives. Buy only on a clean specialist PPI, full build receipts, and a price that stays cheap.
evidence.next_action: Before bidding, book a pre-auction PPI at an independent Bay Area BMW/standalone-EFI specialist (leakdown, cooling pressure test, Haltech datalog, lift inspection of the repaired front clip and shock towers) and simultaneously ask the seller in the comments for the engine build invoices and the configuration of the December 2024 smog certificate.

mission_fit.rationale: It nails the point-of-view half of the enthusiast-bridge brief — manual, rear-drive, LSD, small, analog, exactly the Highway 1 / Carmel Valley Road car described. evidence.next_action: Call an E30-literate independent in the Orlando area today and try to book a lift PPI (strut towers, rear subframe mounts, both front corners with a paint gauge, cooling pressure/block test, timing belt visual) before the 2026-09-10 close — and in the same message ask the seller to post the timing belt invoice and the tire DOT date codes; if the PPI cannot be scheduled, do not bid.

Please post a cold-start video from a genuinely cold engine showing the full key-on bulb check, the cluster after start, idle for two minutes, and coolant temp coming up to normal.
Please run an OBD-II scan and photograph the stored/pending codes and the readiness monitor status — I need to know it will pass a California smog test.
Is the passenger window switch loose because of the switch housing or a failing regulator? Please show both windows going fully up and down in one continuous video.
Does this listing carry a reserve, and if so will you consider a pre-close deal at a number you'd disclose?

Can an independent BMW specialist of my choosing put the car on your lift for a two-hour PPI before the auction closes, given your showroom reopens the morning of 9/8 — or would you extend/relist to allow it?
Any evidence of VANOS rattle at cold idle, and has the VANOS ever been serviced or rebuilt?
Please photograph the odometer and the door-jamb/VIN plate, and confirm the title is in the dealership's name and physically in hand.
ppi_focus: Trunk floor with carpet and spare removed: inspect every spot weld around the differential mounting points for cracking, tearing, prior welding or sealer disguising a repair — this is the pass/fail item
Rear subframe mounting ears and differential finned mount from below on a lift, including whether reinforcement plates are present

Complete cooling system: pressure test, inspect expansion tank for crazing, check water pump for shaft play and weep, thermostat housing, radiator neck, hose condition, and confirm no coolant in the oil
S52 top end: listen for VANOS rattle at cold idle; check valve cover and oil filter housing gasket areas for fresh seepage after the Nov 2025 work
Rear trailing-arm bushings, rear shock mounts/towers, motor and transmission mounts
Clutch engagement point, driveline slop, LSD function and rear diff for leaks
Rocker panels, floor pans, seat mounts and jack points for rust despite the Florida climate
Convertible top mechanism through a full cycle, frame condition, rear window clarity, and the disclosed passenger-side shrinkage
Both window regulators, cluster pixels, dash for cracks, A/C output temperature at idle
Full OBD-II scan for stored codes and readiness monitors, plus tire DOT date codes on all four
what_would_change_verdict: Clear photographs (or a specialist report) showing sound, uncracked trunk-floor spot welds and diff mounting ears — or better, documented reinforcement plates already fitted — would move this from speculative to seriously worth chasing.

Invoices showing a cooling-system refresh (water pump, radiator, expansion tank, thermostat, hoses) within the last few years, plus the itemized Nov 2023/2025 receipts, would lift documentation substantially.
An independent BMW specialist PPI completed before the close, with a clean structural verdict, would justify bidding toward the upper end of the expected range.
Photos showing cracking at the diff mount or trunk-floor welds, or a refusal/failure to produce them before close, would take this off the list at any price above scrap-value bidding.
A hammer price drifting above roughly $16,000 without structural and cooling evidence would defeat the value case entirely — walk at that point.
evidence.mission_note: As a future_keeper this is the right shape of car — factory manual, S52 rather than the rod-bearing S54, LSD, Imola Red, mostly stock — but a keeper is exactly the mission that demands proof of the rear structure and cooling history, and this listing supplies neither. It does nothing for the accelerated_bridge problem either: a 123k-mile roadster with an original-as-far-as-we-know cooling system is not a dependable replacement for the ailing 335i, so buying it would spend cash without solving the actual pressure.
evidence.rationale: This is an appealing, honestly presented, high-mileage M Roadster whose value case currently rests on a $5,750 bid that will not survive two more days. The genuine strengths are structural to the model rather than to this car: the 2000 model year means an S52, so the S54 rod-bearing and double-VANOS liabilities that dominate 2001-02 ownership simply do not apply, and the spec — five-speed, LSD, Imola Red over black Nappa, Style 40 wheels, apparently stock — is on brief. The photos support the cosmetic story: even paint, normal shutlines, clean wheels, a tidy engine bay with no coolant crust, and an underbody free of rust scale. But the single most expensive failure mode on a Z3 M is the trunk-floor and differential-mount weld area, a BaT commenter asked for exactly those photos on day one, and the seller's only reply was that the car would have to go on a lift; nothing has appeared since. Cooling is equally silent — the documented Nov 2025 work covers valve cover and oil pan gaskets, A/C and a heater valve, all oil-and-comfort items, with no radiator, pump, tank or thermostat anywhere in the record, on a 26-year-old car at 123k miles. The listing also establishes two real defects itself: a mismatched Nexen/Sumitomo tire set that must be replaced, and a disclosed shrinking soft-top edge, plus a probable window switch or regulator fault visible to a commenter. The comp evidence says a car like this belongs near the $10,900 Mill Valley 115k-mile result rather than the $20k-$27k low-mileage sales, so there is room to buy well — but only with the structure verified, and the showroom reopens the same morning the auction closes at 10:01am Pacific, which makes a real specialist PPI nearly impossible in the window.
evidence.next_action: Post a public comment today demanding the promised lift photos of the differential mounting ears plus trunk-interior shots of the spot welds with carpet removed, and ask directly whether an independent BMW specialist can lift the car on Tuesday morning 9/8 before the 10:01am Pacific close — bid only if those weld photos come back clean, and cap at roughly $14,000 hammer.

documentation.rationale: Weak on both halves. Identity and terms: no VIN, no odometer photo, no title photo — only a Facebook attribute set (clean title, 2 owners, 192k) and a named private seller with a rating history; the equipment description is detailed and the photos confirm most of it. Maintenance and condition evidence: essentially zero — a bullet list of claimed work (radiator, thermostat, plugs, brakes, filters) with no dates, no mileages, no invoices, no scan, no service history, and no documentation of the suspension install. At 192,000 miles the claim list is the least persuasive form of evidence available.

condition.rationale: Photos genuinely look good: straight panels, consistent grey paint, clean beige leather in all three rows with no bolster collapse or cracked dash, working nav/ML/RSE hardware, matching Falken AT3Ws with real tread, tidy rack and hitch. Against that, this is a 192k-mile first-year GX460 with the three expensive model faults — secondary air injection, KDSS, valley-plate/timing-cover coolant seepage — entirely unaddressed in the ad, plus a lift of unknown install quality on a KDSS chassis, and no underhood, undercarriage or cold-start evidence. Trail photos show the car has actually been used off pavement. Unknowns dominate the areas that cost the most.

price_value.rationale: The asking price is far off the market. A 2010 Premium with 173,709 miles is asking $16,995 in Modesto; a 2010 Premium with 230,000 miles sold for $9,800 in Escondido; a 142,900-mile 2010 sold for $14,250 on Cars & Bids; and a 2017 Premium with 128,500 miles asks $23,900 — the same money as this 2010 with 192,000 miles. Bolt-ons (Ironman kit, rack, AT tires, traction boards) recover pennies on the dollar at resale and, per Jason's brief, add modest value at most. The ad has sat nine weeks at one price with no reduction, which is itself market feedback.

mission_fit.rationale: The capability case is real: body-on-frame, low range, locking centre diff, KDSS, Crawl Control, a full-length roof rack that suits a rooftop tent, a hitch, and a third row — all things the RX 350 cannot supply. But this is also a second large Lexus SUV in the driveway, it is a 192k-mile example rather than a low-risk one, and the mission requires it to justify the overlap on capability and dependability. A cheaper, lower-mileage GX would satisfy the same mission with far less exposure.

logistics.rationale: Mission Viejo is roughly 330 miles from Carmel — a one-day drive or a short flight, and Jason will drive a good car home. Southern California means abundant Toyota/Lexus and GX-specialist shops for a PPI including a KDSS-aware inspection, and the seller has a 20-rating marketplace history. Offsets: PPI access is not addressed in the ad, no VIN is published so nothing can be pre-checked, and a California private-party sale requires the seller to supply a current smog certificate, which is unstated.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Grey over beige with wood trim, Mark Levinson, rear entertainment and a tasteful mild overland build is an attractive, coherent package and photographs well on a fire road. It is also an automatic V8 SUV and makes no claim on the enthusiast brief (MINI/GTI/128i/Z3); its appeal is competence and family utility, not character Jason is chasing.

positives: Genuinely capable spec the RX 350 lacks: KDSS, Crawl Control, low range, full-length roof rack suited to a rooftop tent, hitch and a power third row.
Photographic condition is strong for the mileage — straight panels, consistent grey paint, clean beige leather in all three rows, uncracked dash, intact nav/Mark Levinson/RSE hardware.
Southern California car with a matching set of Falken Wildpeak AT3W all-terrains and a level, modest lift rather than a big cheap one.
Toyota 1UR-FE/J150 platform is exactly what Jason's mechanic recommends and parts/specialist support in California is excellent.
Private seller with a long-standing, highly rated marketplace account within a day's drive, so a specialist PPI before money moves is straightforward to arrange.
concerns: Observed: the price is out of step with the comps — $23,995 for a 192,000-mile 2010 when a 2017 Premium with 128,500 miles asks $23,900 and a 173,709-mile 2010 Premium asks $16,995; it has sat nine weeks with no reduction.
Observed: an Ironman 4x4 lift has been installed over a KDSS chassis with no install invoice, alignment sheet or lean measurement, and the trail photos confirm the truck has been used off pavement.

Observed: every mechanical item is a claim in a bullet list — radiator, thermostat, plugs, brakes — with no date, mileage or receipt behind any of it, and no reason given for the radiator and thermostat replacement.
Unverified: secondary air injection status on a 2010-2012 GX460 (ask for a full OBD scan including stored/pending codes, and any P2440/P2442 history or pump replacement invoice).
Unverified: KDSS leak or cross-corner lean (inspect the valve body, accumulators and sway-bar cylinders for weep and measure lean on level ground).
Unverified: 1UR-FE valley-plate and timing-cover coolant seepage, plus frame and underbody condition (request underhood and undercarriage photos and a lift inspection).
unknowns: VIN — nothing can be decoded, history-reported or recall-checked until it is provided.

Have the transmission, transfer case and front/rear differential fluids been changed, and at what mileage?
Can you send photos of the engine valley/rear of the intake area and of the frame rails and underbody taken on a lift or from underneath?

Do you have a current California smog certificate, and will the sale include one?
What are the DOT date codes on the four Falken tires, and do you have the purchase receipt?
Can you send a cold-start video of at least two minutes, from key-on, with the instrument cluster in frame?
ppi_focus: Secondary air injection: scan for P2440/P2442, check pump operation on cold start and inspect the valves/pump for moisture intrusion.
KDSS: inspect valve body, accumulators and both sway-bar cylinders for hydraulic weep; measure cross-corner lean on level ground and confirm the system still articulates after the lift.
1UR-FE coolant: inspect the valley plate area, timing cover and water pump for seepage; pressure-test the cooling system and check for oil/coolant cross-contamination.
Frame rails, crossmembers and skid areas from below for rust, impact damage or bent components from off-road use.
Lift installation quality: control-arm and shock mounting, CV boot and axle angle, driveshaft/carrier bearing, brake and ABS line routing, and steering geometry/alignment specs.
Transfer case actuator function: shift into 4-Lo and back, confirm no fault codes and no grinding.
Suspension bushings, ball joints, tie rods and rear shocks at 192k miles.
Automatic transmission: fluid condition and level via the check procedure, road-test for shift quality and torque-converter lockup shudder.
Tire DOT date codes and irregular wear pattern that would reveal alignment issues after the lift.
Full body/paint meter check and panel-gap review for unreported collision repair, since no history report exists.
what_would_change_verdict: A clean specialist PPI plus a full scan with no codes, documented healthy KDSS with no lean, and dry valley plate/timing cover — combined with a price renegotiated toward the $15,000-17,000 band the comps support.
Production of dated invoices for the air-injection system, drivetrain fluids and the lift install, converting the claim list into records.
The VIN and a clean history report confirming two owners, no accidents and completed recall work.
Downward: any P2440/P2442 code, visible KDSS hydraulic weep or measurable lean, or coolant seepage at the valley plate — each is four figures on top of an already over-market ask.
Downward: seller declining to release the VIN or to allow a PPI at an independent shop.
evidence.mission_note: This does deliver capability the RX 350 genuinely lacks — body-on-frame, low range, KDSS, roof rack for a rooftop tent, hitch and a third row — so it clears the overlap test on paper. But at 192,000 miles with the three expensive GX460 faults entirely undocumented and an asking price at the level of a 2017 with 64,000 fewer miles, it is not the low-risk capability buy the accelerated_bridge mode calls for at this number.
evidence.rationale: The verdict is driven by price and evidence, not by the truck itself. Condition in the photos is legitimately good: straight grey paint, clean beige leather across three rows, intact Mark Levinson and rear-entertainment hardware, matching Falken AT3Ws and a level, modest lift. But the ad's entire mechanical case is a bullet list — radiator, thermostat, plugs, brakes, filters — with no date, mileage or invoice behind a single line, and at 192,000 miles that is the weakest possible support. Every one of the four model-critical items is missing: no scan for P2440/P2442 secondary air injection, no KDSS leak or lean check on a chassis that has had an Ironman kit installed over it, no underbody or frame images, and no lit-cluster or cold-start evidence. No VIN is published, so no history report, recall check or decode is possible. The market is unambiguous: a 173,709-mile 2010 Premium asks $16,995 in Modesto, a 142,900-mile 2010 sold at $14,250, a 230,000-mile one sold at $9,800, and a 2017 Premium with 128,500 miles asks $23,900 — the same as this. Nine weeks at $23,995 with no reduction confirms the market's read. The build is a modest positive at best under Jason's own rule that accessories never substitute for evidence.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller for the VIN, a recent full OBD scan photo (stored and pending codes), the Ironman install invoice with alignment sheet, and confirmation he will meet at a GX/Toyota specialist in Orange County for a lift PPI — and open the price conversation at the $15,000-17,000 the comps support before booking anything.

contradictions.detail: The same sentence block claims 'Clean interior, exterior and undercarriage' and then 'Has some typical Scout rust.' On a Scout II the typical rust zones (rear quarter kick-ups, floors, tailgate channel, rear spring hangers) are exactly what 'clean undercarriage' would deny. One of the two statements is overstated and only on-lift photos or an inspection can resolve which.

critical_evidence.evidence: No on-lift or underbody imagery in the captured set; the only Scout photo is a driver-side three-quarter exterior. Rear quarter kick-ups, floors and rear spring hangers are unexamined while the seller simultaneously discloses 'some typical Scout rust'.
Captured listing says nothing about current CA registration, plate status, or a recent passing smog certificate. A 1980 gas vehicle requires biennial smog in California.
'New radiator. Rebuilt 727 transmission.' stated with no shop name, date, mileage or invoice. Factory manuals are included but those are literature, not receipts.
No compression or leakdown numbers, no hot oil pressure reading, no cold-start video, no engine bay photo captured for the 304.
'Has some typical Scout rust' is the entire disclosure — no description of what has rotted, what if anything has been cut out and replaced, what panels were used, or who did the work.

documentation.rationale: Both halves of documentation are thin. Identity and terms: a named private seller, a clear location, a firm $29,000 asking price and a model/engine/trans description — but no VIN, no odometer reading, no title statement, so the car cannot be identified or its history checked. Maintenance and condition evidence: two significant claims (rebuilt 727, new radiator) with zero dates, mileages or invoices, and a rust disclosure with no photos or scope. Factory manuals are a nice inclusion but are not service history. Note the capture of this listing is thin, so the seller may hold more than we can see.

condition.rationale: The one Scout photo shows a genuinely attractive truck: straight body lines, glossy brown/white Rallye paint with crisp stripes, correct alloy wheels, healthy-looking BFG all-terrains, stock stance, no visible bubbling in the lower door or front fender. Against that, the seller himself discloses 'some typical Scout rust' — on this model that phrase points straight at the rear quarter kick-up and floors, the two most expensive things to fix — and there is no underside imagery, no mileage, no engine health data and no evidence the cooling system was done as a system rather than a radiator swap. Unknowns in exactly the zones that decide a Scout's value hold this down.

price_value.rationale: $29,000 asking is above the stated max_price of $27,000 before any catch-up work, and the market at that number expects either a fully documented rust-free driver or rust that is disclosed and quantified. Here the rust is disclosed but open-ended, the 727 rebuild and radiator are unreceipted, and mileage is unstated. The Rallye two-tone trim and a claimed one-owner California history are real value adds; the automatic is normal on these and not a penalty. As presented, the rust language is a negotiating lever rather than a description, and the price does not reflect that.

mission_fit.rationale: On character and capability the Scout clears the bar the RX 350 cannot touch: body-on-frame, Dana 44s, Dana 20 transfer case, real fire-road and beach ability, and presence on Carmel Valley Road. But the mission is being served in accelerated_bridge mode, and a 45-year-old carbureted V8 at 10–13 mpg with unquantified rust and no documented recommissioning is a weekend truck, not a car that takes the failing 335i's daily duty. Camping fit is also partial: the fiberglass hardtop is not a straightforward rooftop-tent platform and the cargo box is small for an in-vehicle sleeping platform.

logistics.rationale: San Mateo is roughly a 90-minute drive from Carmel — an easy day trip, in-state title transfer, no transport needed, and the Bay Area has vintage IH/4x4 specialists who can put it on a lift. Seller is flagged responsive. The open items are whether he will release the car for a specialist PPI and whether registration is current with a passing smog certificate, which a 1980 gas vehicle still needs in California.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: This is the desirable presentation: Rallye trim, factory-style two-tone dark brown over white with the black stripe treatment, correct alloys, stock height, no clownish lift or bumper armour. Automatic is period-normal on a Scout and not a demerit here, though a T-19 four-speed would be more special. Strong character, and it is nothing like anything else in the garage.

positives: Desirable Rallye-trim Scout II in factory-style brown/white two-tone with correct alloys and stock stance; the one available photo shows straight, glossy body sides with no visible lower-body bubbling.
Claimed single-owner California car originally sold in San Jose — if documented, that is exactly the provenance that separates a $29k Scout from a $50k restoration project.

Two of the expensive wear items are claimed already addressed (rebuilt TF727, new radiator), and the drivetrain family — IH 304, 727, Dana 20, Dana 44s — is simple, stout and well supported by the aftermarket.
Delivers body-on-frame 4x4 capability and character the RX 350 cannot supply, with an automatic that is period-correct and carries no market penalty on this model.
90 minutes from Carmel, in-state, private seller flagged responsive — a specialist lift inspection is logistically trivial to arrange.
concerns: Observed: the seller discloses 'has some typical Scout rust' with no location, extent, photos or repair history. On this model that phrase points at the rear quarter kick-ups and floors, and proper cut-and-weld repair runs $3,000-$8,000 per side; bondo or fiberglass patching would be disqualifying at this asking price.
Observed: the listing claims a 'clean undercarriage' in the same breath as disclosing rust. Those two statements cannot both be fully true and must be reconciled on a lift before any money moves.
Observed: asking price of $29,000 sits above the stated max_price of $27,000, and it is being asked for a truck whose most value-critical defect is explicitly undefined.

Unverified: no compression, leakdown or hot oil pressure numbers on the 304, and no engine bay photo or cold-start video (ask for a compression/leakdown sheet and a cold-start video showing startup smoke and oil pressure).

Unverified: nothing on the 45-year-old wiring harness, ammeter circuit, fuel tanks/selector valve/steel lines, steering box play or brake system — all documented Scout II failure points and, in the harness case, a fire risk (inspect behind the dash and at the bulkhead connectors).
unknowns: VIN and line-setting ticket — not captured; without them engine, body style and trim cannot be confirmed

seller_questions: Can you put it on a lift or on ramps and send photos of both rear quarter kick-ups, the rear wheelhouses, the rear spring hangers, the rear crossmember and the frame at the body mounts?
Exactly where is the 'typical Scout rust' — name the panels — and has any of it been cut out and replaced? If so, who did the work, what panels were used, and do you have the invoice?
What does the odometer read today, and do you know whether it has ever rolled past 99,999?
What is the VIN, and do you have the original line-setting ticket or window sticker?
Who rebuilt the 727 and when — can you send the invoice showing shop, date and mileage? Same for the radiator.
Will you pull the front carpet or mats so I can see the floor pans and the seat-belt/seat-mount reinforcements in daylight photos?
Is it currently registered in California, and what is the date on the last passing smog certificate?
Would you allow a compression and leakdown test at a shop of my choosing, and can you send a cold-start video from the first crank showing startup smoke and the oil pressure gauge?
Is the carburetor the original Holley or has it been replaced, and is the ignition still points or converted to Pertronix/HEI?
Has the wiring harness ever been replaced, and can you photograph the wiring behind the dash and at the engine-bay bulkhead connector?
What brand are the tires and what are the DOT date codes on the sidewalls?
Beyond the radiator, have the water pump, fan clutch, fan shroud, hoses and heater core been done, and were the fuel tanks, sending units, selector valve and steel lines addressed?
ppi_focus: Full lift inspection by a vintage IH/4x4 specialist with a magnet and a paint depth gauge on both rear quarters, the kick-up area behind the rear wheels, and the rocker/inner-quarter sandwich
Frame rails at the rear spring hangers, rear crossmember and body mount perches; condition of all 12 body mount bushings and the resulting door gaps and hood alignment
Floor pans, footwells and seat-belt/seat-mount reinforcements with carpet lifted; look for fresh undercoating or seam sealer over perforation
Windshield surround under the gasket, cowl, A-pillar corners and tailgate lower channel and drain holes
Compression and leakdown per cylinder on the 304 plus hot oil pressure; check for blue startup smoke, cracked exhaust manifolds and rear main seepage
Cooling system under load in traffic-simulating conditions — fan clutch, presence of the shroud, water pump weep, heater core
Wiring harness brittleness behind the dash and at the bulkhead, ammeter charging circuit, headlight and turn-signal switches; look for Scotch-locks and splices
Steering: Saginaw box play, rag joint, drag link and tie rod ends, box mounting area of the frame; road test for wander at 55 mph
Brakes: master cylinder, all rubber flex lines, rear wheel cylinders, booster function and whether the parking brake actually holds
Fuel system: both side tanks for rust and seepage, sending units, selector valve, steel and rubber lines; sniff for fuel odour in the cabin and under the rear
what_would_change_verdict: On-lift photos or a specialist report showing genuinely solid quarters, floors, frame rails and spring hangers, with any prior rust repair documented as proper cut-and-weld with repro panels — that would move this up substantially.
Itemised invoices for the 727 rebuild and radiator with dates and mileage, plus a stated odometer reading and evidence supporting the one-owner California claim.
A negotiated price that reflects unquantified rust rather than a documented rust-free truck, bringing it inside the stated budget with the catch-up sweep budgeted on top.
Discovery of bondo or fiberglass in the rear quarters, perforated floors, or rot at the rear spring hangers or body mount perches — that is a value cliff and would end it.
Seller declining a lift inspection or unable to show current registration and a passing smog certificate for this 1980 gas vehicle.
evidence.mission_note: As a capability-and-character purchase the Scout II clears the bar the RX 350 cannot — real body-on-frame 4x4, Dana axles, and enormous presence — but it is emphatically not a bridge car for the failing 335i in accelerated_bridge mode: carbureted, 10–13 mpg, and needing a full age-related recommissioning before it is trustworthy daily transport. It should be judged as a discretionary keeper-toy at a correct price, and at $29,000 with undefined rust it is not yet at a correct price.
evidence.rationale: The result is gated on one thing the listing refuses to define: the rust. The seller writes 'clean interior, exterior and undercarriage' and then 'has some typical Scout rust' in the same paragraph — on a Scout II that phrase reliably means the rear quarter kick-ups and floors, the two repairs that convert an affordable truck into an expensive one, and there are no underside photos in the captured set to bound it. The single Scout photo is genuinely encouraging: Rallye trim, straight brown/white two-tone with crisp stripes, correct alloys, healthy-looking BFG all-terrains, stock height, no visible lower-body bubbling. But the two headline mechanical claims — rebuilt 727 and new radiator — arrive with no shop, date, mileage or invoice, no odometer figure is given at all, and there is no VIN, title statement, engine health data, or word on the 45-year-old harness, fuel tanks, steering box or brakes. Market practice on this model is that at $29,000 a buyer is entitled to either a documented, genuinely solid driver or rust that is disclosed with photographs and a number attached; this listing supplies neither, and the asking price already sits above the stated max_price of $27,000. Provenance could be excellent — a one-owner San Jose car with factory manuals is exactly the right story — but it is a story until registration, title and receipts back it. Logistics are the bright spot: San Mateo is a short drive, the seller is responsive, and a Bay Area vintage-4x4 specialist can settle the whole question in two hours on a lift. Until that lift inspection happens, everything that matters about this truck is unknown, and unknown is not good.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller and ask for the VIN, the current odometer reading, and on-lift (or ramp) photos of both rear quarter kick-ups, the floors with carpet lifted, and the rear spring hangers — and if those come back clean, book a pre-purchase inspection with a Bay Area vintage IH/4x4 specialist before discussing price.

condition.rationale: Photo 1 shows a genuinely tidy, ceramic-coated navy truck with even ride height, quality hardware and no visible damage. Fair, not a bargain.

Price movement toward $13,000-$13,500, reflecting the modified-build discount, the missing muffler, the roof clear coat and the undocumented 2023 damage, would improve the value case.

evidence.mission_note: On the utility_capability branch this fits well: body-on-frame 4WD, V8, a sound roof rack, skid plates and cargo space for dogs, gear and a sleeping platform are capability the RX 350 does not provide, and it is 70 miles away with current registration and a fresh smog. It is not the enthusiast bridge — it is an automatic SUV that partially duplicates the household hauler — so it should be judged purely as a capability purchase, and only bought if the V8 off-road/camping capability is itself wanted.
evidence.rationale: This is one of the better-documented GX470s the tracker has seen, and the documents both support and complicate the seller's story. Carfax confirms a clean, unbranded title, no structural damage, four owners, a passed California smog on 4/20/2026, and — importantly — timing belt, tensioner/idler and water pump replaced at 135,475 miles in April 2021, so the belt is roughly 40,500 miles into a 90k interval. But the accompanying Lexus repair order shows that work was not preventive: the belt tore in service ('lost power and steering while driving on hwy,' crank-no-start, cam gears misaligned, 'possible damage to valves'), the water pump was leaking badly, and the RO lists the repair as declined while Carfax shows it completed the next day — so the paid invoice and a compression test are the two things that decide this car. The seller's 'mostly California-driven' rust claim is also contradicted by nine Colorado winters between 2012 and 2021, and RCI skid plates now hide part of the underbody, making a lift inspection mandatory. Against that, seller behaviour is genuinely good: VIN published, dealer records supplied, Carfax offered, and six defects volunteered including the removed muffler, cracked taillight and peeling roof clear coat. The build is brand-name and mission-relevant rather than a cheap lift, though the market discounts overland builds and $15,000 sits at the Carfax value and slightly above the $13,000-$14,000 peer set. Silent areas that matter are the rear height-control air suspension, an apparently original plastic-tank radiator at 176k, undated tires, and the January 2026 'hard to get into gear' complaint the dealer could not reproduce. Everything blocking a decision is answerable in one inspection 70 miles from home.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller for the paid 04/08/2021 Lexus of Greenwood Village invoice and a current OBD scan photo, and simultaneously book a lift PPI at a San Jose Toyota/Lexus specialist with instructions to compression-test the engine and inspect the frame and rear height-control system.

Maintenance-and-condition evidence is the weak half: the 2018 clutch and 2019 $8k cooling service are described in prose with records said to convey, but no invoice, no scan, no borescope report and no DME over-rev printout were available to review, and the 2020-2025 window is documented only by a single oil change. For the one engine risk that defines this model, documentation is empty.

condition.rationale: Presentation is good for 19 years and 70k miles: straight panels with even gaps, unmarked 18" Cayman S wheels, red calipers with cross-drilled rotors, and an exceptionally clean terracotta cabin with no bolster wear or dash cracking visible. The single underbody photo shows a dry, undamaged rear subframe and suspension with only surface grime and light whitish staining, no rot or fresh fluid. Against that, the seller discloses front bumper discoloration and clear-coat failure plus other body blemishes, and states the front strut bump stops are due. The determinative items — cylinder-wall condition on an M97 3.4, AOS, coolant pipes, tire date codes, bushings — are all unexamined, and unknowns on this engine pull hard.

price_value.rationale: Retail asks for 987.1 Cayman S manuals run $35-45k for 24-51k-mile cars, but recent auction reality is softer: 28k-mile S at $27,500 and a 103k-mile S at $23,250 on Cars & Bids, and a 21k-mile base 987.2 at $29,500 on BaT. A 70k-mile, six-owner S with a cosmetic bumper defect, all-season tires of unknown age and no bore evidence should land in the mid-to-high $20s, which sits at the top of the buyer's stated max_price and leaves little room for the engine-verification and catch-up spend a keeper Cayman S demands. The $3,000 current bid on day one carries no information. Excellent spec supports value; the missing borescope caps it.

mission_fit.rationale: As a future keeper this is the right shape of car: manual, mid-engine, PASM, Sport Chrono Plus, sport seats, single long-term owner for the last 7.5 years, and Porsche parts availability. But the profile is explicit that the 3.4 S is bought only with unusually strong engine due diligence, and this listing supplies none, on a 7-day auction clock. It also does nothing for the accelerated_bridge problem — it is a discretionary keeper purchase that consumes the cash reserve while the 335i's coolant and suspension issues remain, and a Cayman S is a poor daily bridge. Attractive only as a keeper, and in direct tension with cash preservation.

logistics.rationale: Centerbrook, CT is a coast-to-coast trip — a cost and a scheduling item, and Jason will fly out and drive a good car home, which suits a sorted Cayman. The real logistics friction is the auction clock: a Porsche-specialist borescope, leakdown and DME pull in Connecticut must be booked and completed before bidding ends Sep 14, and nothing in the listing establishes that inspection access is available. BaT shipping is offered. California registration adds a step: the GMG exhaust's catalytic configuration is unstated, though the original exhaust conveying with the car is a workable path to a visual-inspection pass.

ppi_focus: Specialist borescope of all six cylinders with retained photographs, prioritizing 4-6 for scoring and any evidence of scuffing on the thrust side (this is the go/no-go item).

Front suspension: bump stops the seller flagged, plus strut condition, control-arm and sway-bar bushings, and steering-rack play.
Paint depth readings on all panels and inspection of the front bumper defect for prior repair, plus bumper mounts and radiator-area debris.
Brake rotor cross-drill crack inspection, pad life, and brake-fluid moisture content.
Rear subframe and underbody inspection for the whitish residue visible in photos — confirm it is road film rather than corrosion or a dried fluid trail.
what_would_change_verdict: A dated Porsche-specialist borescope with clear photos of cylinders 4-6 showing no scoring, plus leakdown figures and a clean DME over-rev report, would move this from speculative to a credible keeper.
Posted invoices for an AOS replacement and coolant-pipe inspection, plus documentation of any 2020-2025 service, would lift the documentation and condition ratings materially.
Confirmation that a specialist inspection can actually be completed in Connecticut before the September 14 close — without it, this is an unverifiable M97 bought on prose.

A hammer price near the Cars & Bids reality (low-to-mid $20s) rather than the retail asks would create room for the verification and catch-up spend; a hammer in the $30s makes it uncompetitive against a proven 2.7 manual.
Any borescope showing scoring, an over-rev report with hits in ranges 4-6, or evidence of undisclosed track use would end it outright.
evidence.mission_note: As a future_keeper this is the right kind of car — a rare-spec, long-owned, manual 987.1 Cayman S with the clutch and cooling work claimed done — but the profile's hard gate is a specialist borescope, and this listing supplies zero engine-internals evidence on a 7-day clock. It also does nothing for the accelerated_bridge problem: it is a discretionary keeper that would absorb the cash reserve while the 335i still needs replacing, so it only makes sense if the borescope comes back clean and the hammer stays well under the top of budget.
evidence.rationale: This is an attractive keeper candidate that fails the model's one non-negotiable test as presented. Identity and terms are unusually well documented — VIN, a factory option-code build list confirming PASM, Sport Chrono Plus, P78 sport seats, Bose and the sport shifter, a clean Carfax with six prior owners, a clean AZ title in the seller's name, and a verifiable prior BaT sale of this exact VIN for $23,987 in February 2019 — but the maintenance-and-condition half is prose only. The May 2018 clutch/flywheel and the April 2019 ~$8,000 water pump, thermostat, coolant reservoir and belt service are exactly the right items, yet they are seven years old with only ~8k miles added since, no invoice was reviewable here, and a commenter's question about what has been done since 2020 beyond a November 2025 oil change sits unanswered. Most importantly, this is the M97 3.4 at 70k miles with no borescope, no leakdown and no DME over-rev report, on a car whose owner explicitly brought it east for track time; the profile treats specialist cylinder imaging of 4-6 as a hard requirement and seller assurances of good health are not evidence. Photos support genuinely good condition — straight panels, even gaps, unmarked 18" wheels, a dry undamaged rear subframe, and a terracotta cabin with no visible wear — while the seller honestly discloses front bumper clear-coat failure, other blemishes, and front strut bump stops due, which are the known-work items. Auction comps say a 70k-mile six-owner S without bore evidence belongs in the mid-$20s, not at the $35-45k retail asks, which puts a realistic hammer right at the top of the buyer's price ceiling before any verification or catch-up spend. Spec and emotional fit are close to ideal and the seller is cooperative, so the path forward is inspection access, not rejection. Without a borescope completed before September 14, this is an unverified M97 bought on faith.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller today to arrange a pre-auction Porsche-specialist appointment in the Centerbrook, CT area for a six-cylinder borescope with retained photos of cylinders 4-6, a leakdown test and a PIWIS over-rev/fault pull, and ask him to post the 2018 clutch and 2019 cooling invoices plus tire date codes in the comments; do not bid until those images exist.

Identity and terms are weak-to-middling: named private seller, firm $14,000 price, mileage, colors and a modification list, but NO VIN, no title photo, no history report, and the headline year contradicts the description. Maintenance evidence is the seller's typed list only — eight jobs with mileages but no dates, shops, or a single invoice or receipt photo. The list is specific enough to be credible-sounding, which makes verification more important, not less.

condition.rationale: Photographic evidence is genuinely encouraging as far as it goes: straight black paint with even panel gaps, no visible dents, clean rockers and arches, tidy grey leather with only light bolster sheen, matching deep-tread all-terrains, level stance with no rear sag, and a quality Eibach lift rather than a spacer job. But this is a 198,500-mile body-on-frame Lexus and the attached set contains no engine bay, no undercarriage or frame, no odometer, no cluster, no dashboard top (crack-prone), and no third-row/cargo shot. Headlight lenses are visibly hazed. Unknowns at this mileage pull the number down.

price_value.rationale: $14,000 sits at or slightly above the market this comp set describes: a 176k-mile 2008 asks $15,000 in San Jose, a 195k-mile 2004 SOLD at $13,000 in Oceanside, and a 192k-mile Sport Package car failed to meet reserve at $11,600 on Cars & Bids. The profile is explicit that heavily modified builds trade at a discount to clean stock examples, and 33s plus a lift on 198.5k miles is a modification premium the seller is asking the buyer to pay. The claimed timing belt/water pump/radiator at 179k is worth real money — but only once documented; unpaid-for claims should not be priced as done work.

mission_fit.rationale: For the utility_capability branch this delivers what the RX 350 cannot: body-on-frame construction, full-time 4WD with a locking center diff, a 2UZ V8, a roof basket already mounted for a rooftop tent or gear, and a flat cargo area suited to a sleeping platform. That said, the catch-up note is real — a GX overlaps the RX for family and dog duty, so it only earns its place if the off-pavement and rooftop-tent capability is itself wanted. Fuel consumption at 15 mpg combined and the 33in tires' effect on gearing and ride are the daily costs of that capability.

logistics.rationale: Corona, CA is roughly 300-330 miles from Carmel — an easy fly-or-drive day and a trivially drivable trip home in a functioning GX, and California-legal with no out-of-state registration friction. Toyota/Lexus specialists are plentiful in the Inland Empire, so a PPI should be easy to book, but PPI access, smog certificate status and seller flexibility are all unconfirmed, and no VIN has been released for a pre-trip history pull.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Black over grey with bronze Method wheels, flares and a low-profile roof basket is a tasteful, coherent look rather than a hard-parked overland caricature, and the GX's wood-and-leather cabin still feels like a Lexus. But it is an automatic SUV, not the enthusiast brief — this is explicitly a capability/pragmatic pick, and Jason should not expect it to scratch the MINI/GTI/Z3 itch.

known_work_items: Hazed/yellowed headlight lenses visible in front-three-quarter and head-on photos — restoration or lens replacement
positives: Claimed timing belt, water pump AND radiator all replaced at 179k — the three biggest GX470 money items — leaving roughly 70k miles of belt interval if the receipts exist.

Unusually specific eight-item maintenance narrative from 142k to 179k (control arms, rack and pinion, PS pump, CV axles, tie rods, diff service, front brakes) that fits a genuinely maintained truck rather than a flipped one.
Photos show four matching deep-tread 33in BFGoodrich all-terrains on matching bronze Method wheels plus a full-size matching spare — no mismatched-rubber tax and real trail redundancy.
Level, unsagged stance at all four corners with a quality Eibach Pro-Truck kit rather than a cheap spacer lift; body sits square in both side profiles.
Straight, clean Southern California black paint with even gaps, tidy grey leather, and a roof basket already fitted for the rooftop-tent or gear-hauling camping intent.
300-ish miles from Carmel, California-registered, private seller with a decade-plus profile who corrected his own listing's model year unprompted.
concerns: Observed: the listing headline says 2008 and the description says 2007 — a one-year identity question that also decides whether the 2007+ secondary-air-injection system is in play, and there is no VIN in the ad to settle it.

Observed: $14,000 for 198,500 miles with a lift and 33s sits above a 195k-mile GX that SOLD at $13,000 in Oceanside and a 192k-mile Sport that could not clear $11,600 at auction; the modifications are being priced as value when the profile says they trade at a discount.
Observed: headlight lenses are visibly hazed/yellowed in the front photos — cheap to fix but it is real, established work.

Unverified: every one of the eight claimed repairs, including the timing belt/water pump/radiator at 179k, is a typed sentence with no date, shop or invoice (ask for photographs of all receipts and the belt-service sticker).

Unverified: rear air-spring / height-control status is never mentioned despite a lift being installed — bags could be original at 198.5k, could be delete-converted, could be masked (ask directly and inspect the compressor, bags and AVS lamp).
Unverified: no scan data, no cluster photo and no engine-bay or undercarriage image, so warning lights, oil leaks, exhaust manifold tick and frame condition are all unexamined at nearly 200k miles.
unknowns: VIN — blocks year confirmation, title/accident history, recall status (lower ball joint campaign) and any odometer cross-check.
Whether the rear air suspension bags/compressor are original, replaced, or converted to coils, and whether the AVS/height-control lamp is off.
OBD-II scan results and cluster condition: check engine, VSC/ABS, and any stored codes.
Frame, crossmember and skid-plate condition underneath; the 'no rust' claim has no photo behind it.
Dates on the claimed services — mileage without dates hides how long fluid-sensitive work has been sitting.
Tire DOT date codes; deep tread does not rule out aged rubber on a lifted truck.
Transmission and transfer-case service history — the ad lists a diff service at 173k but no transmission fluid work at any point.
Current smog certificate status and registration currency.
Dashboard-top condition (known GX cracking) and third-row presence/condition.
How long the seller has owned it and whether the pre-142k history is available.
seller_questions: Can you send the VIN so I can pull the history report and confirm the 2007 build year before I drive down?
Can you photograph the actual invoices for the timing belt, water pump and radiator at 179k — I need the shop name and the calendar date, not just the mileage.
Were the rear air suspension bags and the height-control compressor replaced, or converted to coil springs, and at what mileage? If original, do they hold overnight?
Can you send a photo of the instrument cluster with the engine running, and an OBD-II scan screenshot showing no stored or pending codes?
Has the transmission fluid or the transfer case fluid ever been serviced? Your list shows a diff service at 173k but nothing for the trans.
Can you send photos of the frame rails, rear crossmember and the underside of the floor pan taken from underneath, plus one of the engine bay?
What are the DOT date codes on the four BFGs and the spare (the four-digit number on the sidewall)?
Does the truck have a current California smog certificate, and is registration current through what date?
Any oil leaks you're aware of — valve covers, timing cover, rear main — and is there any exhaust manifold tick on a cold start?
Can you send a cold-start video, engine off overnight, showing the first 60 seconds including the dash lights?
Would you allow a pre-purchase inspection at a Toyota/Lexus specialist near Corona, at my expense, before any money moves?
Are the original wheels, tires and any removed stock suspension parts included, and is the third-row seat present?
ppi_focus: Rear air springs, height-control compressor and AVS operation: cycle heights, check for leak-down and for a masked/deleted system behind the Eibach lift.
Verify the timing belt service physically — inspect belt condition and any dated service sticker, check water pump weep hole and the replacement radiator's tanks and hoses.
Full frame and undercarriage inspection: rails, rear crossmember, control-arm mounts and skid plates for corrosion or off-road impact damage.
Lift geometry check: CV axle angles, driveshaft and slip-yoke condition, panhard/track-bar and steering-linkage angles, plus alignment and any tire-edge wear from the 33s.
Lower ball joints (recall history) and steering rack — the rack and PS pump are claimed replaced at 173k, so confirm the parts look recent and dry.
OBD-II scan for stored/pending codes; on a 2007 specifically check the secondary air injection system for pump and valve faults.
Exhaust manifolds for cracks/tick on cold start, and a compression or leak-down check given nearly 200k miles.
Transmission fluid condition and a road test for shift quality, torque-converter shudder and transfer-case center-diff lock engagement.
Paint-depth gauge on all panels and gap check to test the 'no accidents' claim in the absence of a history report.
Dashboard top for cracking, plus power seat, sunroof, rear hatch glass and third-row function.
what_would_change_verdict: Photographed invoices for the 179k timing belt/water pump/radiator plus the 162k-173k suspension work, with dates and shop names, would move documentation and condition up sharply and justify most of the asking price.
A clean specialist PPI showing healthy rear air suspension (or a documented quality coil conversion), no stored codes, dry engine and a rust-free frame would make this a strong capability buy.
VIN release confirming a 2007 build, clean title and no reported accidents removes the identity question entirely.
Discovery of sagging/leaking rear bags, a masked AVS light, an oil leak at the rear main, or evidence of hard off-road use under the skid plates would push this down and out at $14,000.
Seller declining a PPI or refusing the VIN would end it regardless of how good the photos look.
evidence.mission_note: This is a legitimate utility_capability candidate: body-on-frame, full-time 4WD, V8, roof basket and flat cargo floor give Jason camping and trail capability the RX 350 genuinely cannot supply, and Corona is an easy retrieval. But it duplicates the RX for family/dog duty, so it only earns the driveway spot if the off-pavement and rooftop-tent use is actually wanted — and it does nothing for the enthusiast brief, so it does not substitute for the MINI/GTI/Z3 search.
evidence.rationale: The single most valuable thing in this ad — timing belt, water pump and radiator done at 179k, i.e. 19,500 miles ago — is exactly the claim that must not be taken on trust, and the seller supplied no dates, no shop names and no receipts for it or for the other seven jobs. What the photographs do establish is good: straight black paint with even gaps, clean rockers and arches on a Southern California truck, grey leather with only light wear, four matching deep-tread 33in BFGs on matching Method wheels plus a full-size matching spare, and a level unsagged stance on a quality Eibach Pro-Truck kit rather than a cheap spacer lift. What they do not show is anything that matters mechanically at 198,500 miles: no engine bay, no undercarriage or frame, no odometer, no instrument cluster, and no mention anywhere of the rear air springs or height-control system despite a lift having been installed — the second of the profile's two biggest price drivers is simply absent from the conversation. The listing also contradicts itself on year, headline 2008 versus the seller's own '2007 NOT a 2008', and there is no VIN to settle it or to pull a history report. On price, $14,000 asks more than the 195k-mile Oceanside car that sold at $13,000 and well more than the 192k-mile Sport that stalled at $11,600, and the profile warns that modified builds discount rather than premium against clean stock examples. Hazed headlights are the only defect the evidence actually establishes. The seller reads cooperative — he corrected his own year, he has a long-standing profile, and he is buying a GX550, which is a coherent reason to sell — so the fix here is cheap: VIN, receipt photos, a scan, and a specialist PPI.
evidence.next_action: Message the seller for the VIN plus photographed invoices for the 179k timing belt/water pump/radiator, and ask directly whether the rear air bags are original, replaced or coil-converted — then, if those answers hold, book a Toyota/Lexus specialist PPI near Corona before traveling.

documentation.rationale: Identity and terms are solid: full VIN, stock number 10025, itemised price stated to include fees, a published price history, an AutoCheck summary (clean title, 0 accidents reported, 5 owners), a detailed factory equipment list, and a named dealer with a phone number. What is entirely absent is the second half — maintenance and condition evidence. Zero receipts, no cooling-system history, no undercarriage or trunk-floor photographs, no scan data, no statement that records accompany the car. On a Z3 M the market pays for documentation more than for mileage, and there is none here.

condition.rationale: The visible cosmetics are genuinely good: Imola Red paint with clean, undistorted reflections across the hood and doors, straight panel gaps at the front, unmarked M double-spoke wheels, no curb rash on the front wheel close-up, clean black interior with the top stowed. But everything that actually determines whether this is a good Z3 M is unexamined here — rear subframe/trunk-floor welds, differential mount, cooling plastics, soft-top mechanism, trailing-arm bushings, rear shock mounts, tire dates. 30,959 miles across 28 years and five owners means the car has sat far more than it has driven, which is hard on seals, hoses, tires and the top, and there is no service evidence to offset that. Photo-good, evidence-empty.

price_value.rationale: At $21,353 with fees included, this sits mid-pack against the comps: a 29,120-mile 1999 sold on BaT at $23,500, a 34,400-mile 2000 sold at $27,000 on Cars & Bids, a 14,600-mile 1999 sold at $27,995 in Mission Viejo, while a 33,000-mile 2000 went reserve-not-met at $14,600 and mid-mileage roadsters trade $17,900-$24,000. So the ask is fair-to-slightly-favourable on mileage alone, and 85 days on the lot plus a $4,665 slide from the original $26,018 says the market has not been in a hurry. The offset is that with no records, cooling refresh and a rear-structure inspection have to be priced in as near-certain spend, and undocumented Z3 Ms resell to enthusiasts at a discount.

mission_fit.rationale: As a future_keeper this is squarely on the profile list — a factory-manual S52 M Roadster, the more robust of the two Z3 M engines, no rod-bearing exposure, in a desirable colour. It is not a bridge car: a fair-weather two-seat roadster with no service history does not replace the 335i's daily duty, and buying it now spends the middle of the budget on a car whose real cost is not knowable until a specialist has been under it. Attractive as a keeper, in tension with the accelerated_bridge cash-preservation logic, and it would leave Jason still shopping for the actual bridge.

logistics.rationale: Joliet, IL is a fly-out-and-drive-home proposition, which the buyer accepts, and a fixed dealer address makes a specialist PPI arrangeable in principle — Chicago has good BMW independents who know the Z3 M rear structure. Against that: PPI access is not offered or confirmed, the dealer is a high-volume exotic house with a 3.3/5 rating over 124 reviews and no evident interest in this car's history, and a 1998 gasoline car imported into California needs a passing smog certificate with no readiness or test data provided. A 2,100-mile drive home in an un-inspected 28-year-old car with unknown cooling and unknown tire dates is not the way to do it; transport or a post-PPI drive is.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Imola Red over black, factory five-speed, S52 M Roadster with the fender gills, roadster hood and the chrome-ringed M kidney — this is exactly the character the buyer likes, and it is one of the cars named in his own shortlist family. Low indicated mileage and apparently stock presentation help. Half a point off for the painted calipers and the stick-on grille stripes, small departures from stock on a car where originality is part of the appeal, and because the coupe, not the roadster, is the variant that carries the real long-term emotional and value weight.

positives: Correct core specification for a keeper: factory 5-speed manual S52 M Roadster, 240 hp, so the S54 rod-bearing and double-VANOS liabilities simply do not apply to this car.
Identity and terms are fully disclosed — VIN, stock number, price stated to include fees, published price history, and an AutoCheck summary showing clean title and no reported accidents.
Imola Red over black with M double-spoke wheels; paint in the studio photos shows clean, undistorted reflections across hood and doors, tight front panel gaps, and no curb rash on the wheel shown.

Priced mid-pack for the mileage against comps (29,120-mile 1999 at $23,500 BaT; 34,400-mile 2000 at $27,000 C&B), with 85 days on the lot and a $4,665 cumulative reduction indicating real negotiating room.
Appears mechanically stock — no evidence of tuning, exhaust or suspension modification, and the only recall on file is an aftermarket-lamp campaign that does not apply to factory lighting.
concerns: Observed: five previous owners against 30,959 miles — roughly 1,100 miles a year with frequent turnover. Long storage periods are hard on cooling plastics, seals, tires and the convertible top, and nothing in the ad explains the ownership churn.
Observed: no service history of any kind is offered, and the selling dealer is a high-volume exotic house (3.3/5, 124 reviews) with no apparent knowledge of the car's maintenance past.

Unverified: rear subframe / trunk-floor spot welds and the differential mount, the Z3 M's defining structural failure (ask for underbody and trunk-floor photos and a specialist PPI; reinforcement plates already fitted would be a strong positive).
Unverified: cooling system — radiator, expansion tank, water pump, thermostat, hoses. Assume original until invoices say otherwise (ask for receipts or plan a full refresh).
